— The São Paulo race Paraná Pesquisas has Governor Tarcísio de Freitas on 50% and Fernando Haddad on 33.8%, a gap of just over 16 points.

— The method Brasília fieldwork ran 14-18 August with a 2-point error margin; São Paulo ran 16-18 August with 2.4 points.

The eye-catching Flavio Bolsonaro lead over Lula comes from Brasília alone, a right-leaning enclave, not from Brazil as a whole.

Illustrative photo: Celina Leão at a Brasília government ceremony handing over police vehicles. She leads the Federal District governor race with 34% in the Real Time Big Data survey of 14-18 August 2026. (Photo: Agência Brasília, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Two fresh Brazil election polls landed this week, and both carry a warning label. In Brasília, Celina Leão leads the race for governor and Michelle Bolsonaro leads for the Senate.

In São Paulo, Governor Tarcísio de Freitas sits on 50%, some 16 points clear of Fernando Haddad.

What the Brasília Poll Found

Real Time Big Data surveyed 1,600 voters in Brazil’s Federal District between 14 and 18 August. Celina Leão, the sitting governor, leads the race to keep her job with 34%.

Former governor José Roberto Arruda follows on 22%, while Leandro Grass of the Workers’ Party takes 18%. Paula Belmonte has 6% and Ricardo Cappelli has 5%.

Blank and spoiled ballots account for 6%, and another 8% of voters are undecided. The margin of error is two percentage points, at 95% confidence.

The Senate Race in the Capital

Michelle Bolsonaro, the former first lady, leads the Senate contest with 25%. This is her first run for office, and she stands for the Liberal Party.

Leila Barros follows on 17%. Bia Kicis and Erika Kokay are tied on 15%, so the fight for the second seat still looks wide open.

The Federal District elects two senators in October. Because voters pick two names, more than one of these candidates can win a seat.

Bia Kicis also runs for the Liberal Party, so the two allies share a base. Erika Kokay, a Workers’ Party veteran, holds the left flank.

Why the 44-39 Runoff Number Is Not National

The same survey also asked about a presidential runoff. Flávio Bolsonaro took 44% against 39% for President Lula, a five-point gap.

However, that question went to the same 1,600 Brasília voters. It is a Federal District result, and it is not a national one.

The distinction matters, because the capital leans well to the right of Brazil as a whole. Reading it as a nationwide verdict would be a mistake.

In the first round in Brasília, the two men are almost level. Lula has 36% and Flávio Bolsonaro has 35%.

How These Brazil Election Polls Compare With National Ones

National Brazil election polls this month tell a different story. Quaest, released on 14 August, had Lula on 43% and Flávio Bolsonaro on 40%.

BTG/Nexus, released three days later, put Lula on 47% and Flávio on 44%. Both gaps sit inside the margin of error, so the national race is effectively tied.

By contrast, the Brasília figure flips the order around. That is what a regional stronghold looks like once you break the numbers down.

Brazil holds a runoff only if nobody wins half the valid votes nationally. Local samples therefore say little about who eventually takes the presidency.

São Paulo: Tarcísio Well Clear of Haddad

Paraná Pesquisas polled 1,680 voters across 80 São Paulo municipalities from 16 to 18 August. Governor Tarcísio de Freitas leads with 50%.

Fernando Haddad, the former finance minister, has 33.8%. The gap is a little over 16 points, and it is far wider than the survey’s error margin.

In a simulated runoff, Tarcísio takes 53% to Haddad’s 36.9%. The margin of error is 2.4 points, and the poll is registered as SP-08913/2026.

Is Tarcísio Running for President?

No. Tarcísio registered with the electoral court as a candidate for re-election as governor of São Paulo. Registrations closed on 15 August, so the field is now fixed.

Despite years of speculation, he is not on the presidential ballot. The Liberal Party’s presidential candidate is Flávio Bolsonaro instead.

His father, Jair Bolsonaro, is ineligible and cannot run this year.

Who Is Celina Leão?

Celina Leão was elected vice-governor in 2022 on Ibaneis Rocha’s ticket. She took the top job on 30 March 2026, after he stepped down to chase a Senate seat.

Ibaneis later abandoned that bid. Celina Leão therefore goes into October as an incumbent with only a few months in the chair.

The Arruda Question

José Roberto Arruda governed the Federal District from 2007 to 2010. He left office during the Caixa de Pandora corruption scandal and was later convicted of administrative misconduct.

His party launched him anyway. Still, the courts have not settled whether the Clean Record law bars him, so his place on the ballot remains uncertain.

How the Two Surveys Were Run

Brazilian pollsters must register each survey with the electoral court before publication. The Brasília study carries registration DF-07849/2026 for the state races.

Its presidential question was filed separately as BR-05423/2026, even though it used the same 1,600 local respondents. Real Time Big Data paid for the work itself.

Paraná Pesquisas also funded its own São Paulo survey. Face-to-face interviews covered 80 municipalities, and the confidence level is 95%.

What Happens Next

Brazilians vote on 4 October, with runoffs on 25 October where no one clears half the valid votes. About 158.7 million voters are registered nationally.

More Brazil election polls will land through September, so these numbers will move. For now, treat the Brasília runoff figure as a local snapshot rather than a national verdict.

The capital holds only a small slice of Brazil’s electorate. Even a landslide there barely moves a national total of 158.7 million registered voters.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the 44% to 39% runoff result a national poll?

No. It comes from Real Time Big Data’s survey of 1,600 voters in Brazil’s Federal District only. National polls in August put Lula narrowly ahead of Flávio Bolsonaro.

Is Tarcísio de Freitas running for president in 2026?

No. He registered as a candidate for re-election as governor of São Paulo before the 15 August deadline. Paraná Pesquisas tested him for the governorship, not the presidency.

Who leads the Federal District Senate race?

Michelle Bolsonaro, on 25%. Leila Barros has 17%, while Bia Kicis and Erika Kokay are tied on 15%.

When does Brazil vote?

The first round is on 4 October 2026. Runoffs for president and state governors take place on 25 October 2026.

Sources: Poder360; Metrópoles; R7; UOL; Gazeta do Povo.

World.title: Brazil Justices Push to Revisit the Journalism Degree Requirement
World.content:
Brazil · Media

Key Facts — The date On August 18, 2026, Justices Alexandre de Moraes and Flavio Dino said in open session that Brazil’s Supreme Court should debate the diploma rule again.

— The setting Their remarks came in a First Panel case about a right of reply won by a Rio clinic against TV Globo and its news site G1.

— The precedent In June 2009 the full court struck the rule down 8-1 in RE 511961, with Gilmar Mendes as rapporteur and only Marco Aurelio dissenting.

— The status There is no new case, no vote and no majority; Justice Carmen Lucia asked for extra time in the Globo case, pausing it.

— The other route PEC 206/2012, passed by the Senate in 2012, has sat ready for a floor vote in the Chamber and needs 308 votes in two rounds.

No case has been filed and no vote has been cast, so the 2009 ruling that freed the profession still stands.

Illustrative photo: the Justice statue outside Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court in Brasilia, where the court voted 8-1 in June 2009 to strike down the journalism diploma rule. (Photo: Dasfour2022, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Brazil’s Supreme Court has not restored the journalism degree requirement, and nothing about the law changed this week. Two justices simply said out loud, in open session on August 18, 2026, that the country should argue about it again.

Those were spoken opinions in an unrelated case, not votes.

What Actually Happened in Court

The First Panel of Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court met on August 18, 2026. It was hearing an appeal by TV Globo and G1 against a right-of-reply order won by a Rio de Janeiro clinic.

During the debate the conversation drifted to who counts as a journalist. Justices Alexandre de Moraes and Flavio Dino then said the court should look again at the diploma rule it scrapped in 2009.

Neither man cast a vote on diplomas, because no diploma case was before them. Their votes that day went to upholding the clinic’s right of reply.

The panel did not finish. Justice Carmen Lucia asked for more time to study the file, which suspends the judgment until she returns it.

Why the Journalism Degree Requirement Fell in 2009

The journalism degree requirement came from Decree-Law 972 of 1969, written under military rule. It obliged anyone practising journalism to hold a university degree in the field and register with the labour ministry.

On June 17, 2009, the full court ruled 8-1 in Recurso Extraordinario 511961 that the 1988 Constitution had not absorbed that rule. Gilmar Mendes was the rapporteur, and Marco Aurelio was the lone dissenter.

The reasoning was blunt. Journalism is an exercise of free expression.

So demanding a state-approved diploma to speak was treated as a restriction the Constitution does not allow. Judges also leaned on Article 13 of the American Convention on Human Rights.

Since then, anyone in Brazil may work as a journalist without a degree, and appeals against the ruling were rejected in 2019.

What Moraes Said From the Bench

Moraes reached for a historical parallel. Early last century Brazil let unqualified advocates known as rabulas practise law.

And that was phased out with a transition rule for those already working. He argued that social media has created the same problem in reverse.

Anyone can wake up, declare themselves a journalist, and start attacking reputations from a blog, in his description. So, he said, perhaps it is time to reflect again, with protection for people who already do the job seriously.

He framed it as regulating a profession like any other in Brazil. He did not spell out whether that means a compulsory degree, a licence, or something looser.

No draft text exists, and no proposal has been filed at the court.

What Dino Said From the Bench

Dino was working through a narrower worry about legal protections. Because press guarantees are strong, he said, extending them automatically to any blogger creates an obvious loophole.

He put it vividly. Warning that criminal groups such as the PCC and Comando Vermelho could hold a contest to pick their own bloggers.

Shielding those people as journalists would then be absurd, in his view. He also said that the 2009 decision, which he respects, might one day be debated again.

That single sentence is what set off two days of headlines in Brazil. Dino has separately argued that a reporter’s duty to protect a source is not absolute.

That claim matters, because it runs alongside a live dispute over one of his own cases.

The Rapporteur of the 2009 Ruling Now Says Rediscuss

The most striking response came from inside the court. Gilmar Mendes wrote the 2009 opinion, and on August 19, 2026, he told reporters in Brasilia that the ruling could be reopened.

He said the decision waived the diploma but never waived training, since people could bring qualifications from many fields. Still, he added, the court can rediscuss it if information quality is genuinely suffering.

He also cautioned against drawing a firm conclusion from one episode. He was referring to a serious dispute in Maranhao state that has dominated the debate.

Even so, a rapporteur inviting a rethink of his own precedent is unusual. It is the clearest signal yet that the question is no longer settled inside the court.

The Backdrop: A Search Order and a Reporter’s Source

None of this arrived out of nowhere. On August 11, 2026, federal police searched the home of Raimundo Cutrim.

A former Maranhao state secretary, on an order signed by Moraes. Investigators treat Cutrim as the source behind reporting by journalist Luis Pablo about official cars used by Dino’s family.

Press bodies read the operation as an attack on source confidentiality. Moraes defended the order, drawing a line between protecting a source and taking part in a crime.

Meanwhile, court president Edson Fachin publicly backed press freedom and source secrecy. Fachin signalled that Moraes’s decision should go to the full court.

Therefore the diploma comments landed in a week already loaded with press-freedom tension.

How Brazil’s Press Bodies Reacted

The journalists’ federation FENAJ welcomed the opening. Its president, Samira de Castro, said no decision has aged as badly as the one that abolished the diploma requirement.

FENAJ has campaigned for the rule’s return for seventeen years. It says either Congress or the court could fix what it sees as a mistake.

And it offered to help with the debate. Newspaper publishers were colder.

Marcelo Rech of the national newspaper association ANJ called it strange to reopen the topic while justices defend piercing a journalist’s confidentiality. As if the end justified the means.

Abraji, the investigative journalism association, kept its focus on source protection as a constitutional guarantee. In short, the industry is split, and the split does not follow the usual left-right lines.

The Route Through Congress

There is a legislative path that has existed for years. The Senate approved a constitutional amendment restoring the diploma in two rounds, by 65-7 in November 2011 and 60-4 in August 2012.

It moved to the Chamber of Deputies as PEC 206/2012 and cleared the constitutional affairs committee in 2013. Since then it has sat ready for a floor vote that never gets scheduled.

A constitutional amendment needs 308 votes in the Chamber, twice. That is a high bar, and no party has spent political capital on it.

Congress could act tomorrow without any help from the court. Yet the practical reality is that the proposal has been parked for more than a decade.

What Would Change if the Rule Returned

Today the answer is simple: nothing has changed. Anyone may report, edit, film or publish in Brazil without a degree or a state register.

If the rule returned, employers would have to check credentials before hiring newsroom staff. Moraes has floated a transition rule so people already working would keep their jobs.

The harder question is what happens to everyone outside a newsroom. Bloggers, podcasters, YouTubers and independent newsletter writers would face a line between protected journalism and ordinary speech.

Brazil has about 295 active undergraduate journalism programmes, according to an April 2026 count by the teaching association ABEJ. A restored rule would make those courses the gateway to the trade.

What to Watch Next

First, watch for a case. Nothing can change until someone files a suit that squarely asks the court to overturn the 2009 ruling.

Second, watch Carmen Lucia. Her return of the Globo file will show whether the panel wants to write anything broad about who deserves press protection.

Third, watch the Chamber. If leaders suddenly schedule PEC 206/2012, the court becomes a sideshow rather than the main stage.

Until one of those happens, the position is unchanged. The journalism degree requirement remains unconstitutional in Brazil, and only a new majority or a new amendment can alter that.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has Brazil reinstated the journalism degree requirement?

No. As of August 19, 2026, the 2009 ruling stands, and no degree is needed to work as a journalist in Brazil. Two justices only said the question deserves a fresh debate.

Did Moraes and Dino vote to bring the diploma back?

No. They spoke during a First Panel hearing on a right-of-reply appeal by TV Globo. Their votes in that case were about the right of reply, not about diplomas.

What did the 2009 decision actually say?

In RE 511961, decided 8-1 on June 17, 2009. The court held that the 1988 Constitution did not absorb the 1969 decree requiring a journalism degree and labour ministry registration.

Could Congress restore the requirement instead?

Yes. PEC 206/2012 already passed the Senate and awaits a floor vote in the Chamber of Deputies.

Sources: Folha de S.Paulo; Poder360; Agencia Brasil; O Povo; Supremo Tribunal Federal.

World.title: A Peruvian Student Built a Free ‘Tinder for Scholarships’ — 15,000 Have Used It
World.content:
Peru · Education

Key Facts Who built it Raúl Jáuregui Penny, a 22-year-old environmental engineering student at the Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia in Lima.

Raúl Jáuregui Penny, a 22-year-old environmental engineering student at the Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia in Lima. What it is called Becas para Migajear, and it runs in a browser at rauenciencia.com. There is no app to download.

Becas para Migajear, and it runs in a browser at rauenciencia.com. There is no app to download. How it works You swipe: right to keep an offer, left to discard it, and you end up with a shortlist. That is where the Tinder name comes from.

You swipe: right to keep an offer, left to discard it, and you end up with a shortlist. That is where the Tinder name comes from. It is free There is no charge, and the listings are public offers from governments, universities and international bodies, sorted with help from AI.

There is no charge, and the listings are public offers from governments, universities and international bodies, sorted with help from AI. The scale so far More than 15,000 young people in Peru, Mexico and Chile have used it, with a reach the founder puts at over 400,000.

More than 15,000 young people in Peru, Mexico and Chile have used it, with a reach the founder puts at over 400,000. How many offers Andina reported about 200 opportunities in the pool with a target of 500; Jáuregui has since said a newer version passes 500.

Andina reported about 200 opportunities in the pool with a target of 500; Jáuregui has since said a newer version passes 500. How fast It went from launch to that user base in about three months.

Scholarship money is not hard to find because it is scarce. It is hard to find because nobody keeps a list.

There is a specific kind of frustration familiar to anyone who has tried to fund a degree abroad. The money exists. Governments offer it, universities offer it, international organisations offer it. What nobody offers is a single place to look. A 22-year-old in Lima got tired of that and built one: a Tinder for scholarships, with the cheerfully self-deprecating name Becas para Migajear — roughly, scholarships for scrounging.

Becas para Migajear filters public scholarship offers down to the ones a student qualifies for. (Photo internet reproduction)

Why a Tinder for scholarships, and not a list

Raúl Jáuregui Penny studies environmental engineering at the Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia. He knows the terrain: he grew up in extreme poverty in eastern Lima, got to university on a Pronabec Beca 18 state scholarship, and has won fifteen scholarships and exchanges himself. Like most students who go looking for funding, he found the information scattered across ministry pages, university notice boards and embassy PDFs, each with its own deadlines and no way to compare them.

So he built a platform that gathers those public offers in one place and uses AI to sort and check them, then filters against what you tell it about yourself — what you study, where you are, what level you are at. Instead of reading eighty announcements to find the two that apply to you, you see the two.

The Tinder comparison is his, and it is literal rather than romantic: you swipe right to keep an offer and left to discard it, and finish with a shortlist. On how many offers there are, the accounts differ slightly — the state news agency Andina reported about 200 in the pool with a goal of 500, while Jáuregui told another outlet a day earlier that a newer version already passes 500. It runs in a browser at rauenciencia.com, with no app to install.

What it has done so far

In roughly three months the platform has been used by more than 15,000 young people in Peru, Mexico and Chile, with a reach the founder puts at over 400,000 — a social-media figure rather than a user count, so read it as attention, not sign-ups. For a free tool built by one undergraduate, that is still a lot of people who could not find what they were looking for.

It is worth being clear about what it is and is not. It does not award scholarships. It gathers, checks and filters offers that are already public. The applications, the deadlines and the paperwork are still yours to handle.

It has grown almost entirely through social media, where Jáuregui posts as Raw en Ciencia, rather than through any school or ministry — which is both how it reached 15,000 people in three months and the reason many of the students who need it most have still never heard of it.

Why this matters if you are raising a family here

For expatriate and Latin American families alike, the cost of higher education is one of the two or three numbers that shape where you live. Scholarships change that arithmetic, but only if you know they exist, and information about them is unevenly distributed in a way that quietly favours whoever already has a well-connected school counsellor.

A free filter does not fix that. It does narrow the gap slightly, and it does so for a teenager in Iquitos on the same terms as one in Lima. If you have a child approaching university, or you are considering a postgraduate degree yourself while living in the region, it costs nothing to look.

The broader point is one worth noticing. The most useful pieces of technology in Latin America this decade have not been the funded ones. They have been small, practical fixes to problems the people building them were personally living with — and this is a textbook example.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Tinder for scholarships? It is Becas para Migajear, a free platform created by Raúl Jáuregui Penny, a 22-year-old environmental engineering student at the Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia in Lima. You enter a study profile and then swipe through publicly available scholarship offers — from governments, universities and international organisations — keeping the ones you qualify for. It runs in a browser at rauenciencia.com, with no app to download. Does it cost anything? No. The platform is free to use, and the scholarships it lists are public offers rather than paid placements. It does not award funding itself; it gathers, checks and filters announcements that are already open, and you still make each application directly. How many people have used it? More than 15,000 young people in Peru, Mexico and Chile in roughly three months since launch, with a reach the founder puts at over 400,000 — a social-media reach figure rather than a user count. Andina reported about 200 opportunities in the pool with a goal of 500; Jáuregui has since said a newer version exceeds 500. Is it only for Peruvians? No. Users are reported in Peru, Mexico and Chile, and the scholarships aggregated include offers from foreign governments, universities and international organisations in Europe and the United States, which are typically open to applicants across the region rather than to one nationality.

Sources: El Peruano — Peruvian student creates a Tinder for scholarships; Stakeholders — Becas para Migajear, the Peruvian platform connecting students to scholarships

World.title: Free Street Art Takes Over Belo Horizonte Until August 30
World.content:
Brazil · Culture

Key Facts Free, all of it CURA 2026 runs from 19 to 30 August in central Belo Horizonte, and there is no ticket for any part of it.

CURA 2026 runs from 19 to 30 August in central Belo Horizonte, and there is no ticket for any part of it. A farewell This is the ninth CURA in Belo Horizonte and the last one built around Praca Raul Soares, which has anchored the festival since 2021.

This is the ninth CURA in Belo Horizonte and the last one built around Praca Raul Soares, which has anchored the festival since 2021. Two big names Ailton Krenak, the Indigenous writer and thinker, and the artist Monica Nador sign this year’s building-side murals.

Ailton Krenak, the Indigenous writer and thinker, and the artist Monica Nador sign this year’s building-side murals. Four walls, not two Krenak takes the Pignataro building at Avenida Augusto de Lima 869 and Nador the Florenca at Rua Guaranis 555, with Binho Barreto on the Sesc Palladium facade and Rafaela Ianni on the JK playground wall.

Krenak takes the Pignataro building at Avenida Augusto de Lima 869 and Nador the Florenca at Rua Guaranis 555, with Binho Barreto on the Sesc Palladium facade and Rafaela Ianni on the JK playground wall. The public week The programme in the square itself — music, workshops, artists at work — runs 26 to 30 August.

The programme in the square itself — music, workshops, artists at work — runs 26 to 30 August. Rooftop tours From 27 to 30 August at 4.30pm you can go up the Edificio JK for a guided view. Free, no booking — passes are handed out at the door 30 minutes before, first come first served.

From 27 to 30 August at 4.30pm you can go up the Edificio JK for a guided view. Free, no booking — passes are handed out at the door 30 minutes before, first come first served. This year’s theme “Descansar Enquanto” — roughly, resting while. Make of it what you like; the artists have.

For twelve days the tallest walls in Belo Horizonte become canvases, and you do not pay a cent to watch it happen.

If you are anywhere near Belo Horizonte over the next twelve days, the city is giving you one of the better free shows in Brazil. CURA 2026 Belo Horizonte — the name is short for Circuito Urbano de Arte — started on Wednesday, and between now and 30 August a handful of enormous blank walls in the middle of town will turn into paintings you can see from three blocks away.

Large-scale street murals in Brazil. CURA 2026 paints four walls in central Belo Horizonte. (Photo internet reproduction)

What CURA 2026 Belo Horizonte actually is

The idea is simple and slightly mad. Every year the festival picks a few tall buildings downtown, gets permission for the side walls, and hands them to artists working from cranes. The result is a permanent open-air gallery: past editions are still up, still part of the daily walk to work for thousands of people.

This is the ninth edition in Belo Horizonte, and it carries a note of farewell — organisers have described it as the last one centred on Praca Raul Soares, which the festival has used since 2021. If you have been meaning to see CURA in the square, this is the year.

The two artists worth planning around

The name that will travel furthest is Ailton Krenak — writer, philosopher, Indigenous leader, and the first Indigenous person elected to the Brazilian Academy of Letters. He is not someone you associate with a downtown wall, and this is his first work at this scale. It is why this edition is getting national attention.

Alongside him is Monica Nador, who has spent decades making painting collectively, with communities, in the places where people actually live. Putting her and Krenak on the same skyline is a statement about who gets to decorate a city.

Six more artists — Tina Soul, Efe Godoy, Nica, Dalata, Tot and Fhero — fill out the public programme, painting live in the square on 26 and 27 August.

How to see it without wasting a day

Painting began on 19 August, so the walls are live now. To watch artists at work, come to the square on 26 or 27 August, when the six square artists paint live. The run closes with the Festa Honk on 30 August, 2pm to 8pm, and a play street for children on 29 and 30.

The two addresses to put in your phone are Avenida Augusto de Lima 869 and Rua Guaranis 555. Both are walkable from Praca Raul Soares, and both are best seen from across the street rather than from underneath.

The rooftop visit is the one to arrive early for. From 27 to 30 August at 4.30pm, guided groups go up the Edificio JK — Oscar Niemeyer’s building, and the best vantage point in the centre. There is no booking: passes are handed out at the door 30 minutes beforehand, first come first served.

Why this matters if you live in Latin America

Public art is one of the few things a city gives its residents that does not depend on income. You need no membership, no reservation and no Portuguese to stand on a corner and look at a forty-metre painting. If you have just moved to Brazil and are still working out how to spend a Saturday, that is a cheap afternoon with a high return.

It also says something about Belo Horizonte. Brazil’s third-largest metropolitan area is regularly skipped by visitors heading straight from Rio to the coast, and the city has spent a decade using culture to argue otherwise. CURA is the most visible part of that argument.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is CURA 2026 free? Yes. There is no ticket for any part of CURA 2026, including the murals and the public programme in Praca Raul Soares from 26 to 30 August. The guided rooftop visits to the Edificio JK are free too, with no booking — passes are handed out at the door 30 minutes before each 4.30pm session, first come first served. When exactly does CURA 2026 run? Painting began on 19 August 2026 and the festival runs to 30 August. The public programme in Praca Raul Soares runs from 26 to 30 August, and the guided rooftop visits to the Edificio JK take place from 27 to 30 August at 4.30pm. Who is painting this year? Ailton Krenak, the Indigenous writer and member of the Brazilian Academy of Letters, and the artist Monica Nador are creating the 2026 building-side murals. The public programme also features Tina Soul, Efe Godoy, Nica, Dalata, Tot and Fhero.

World.title: Free Mozart Near Buenos Aires: Six Nights of The Magic Flute in La Plata
World.content:
Argentina · Opera

Key Facts Six performances Friday 21, Saturday 22 and Sunday 23 August, then Friday 28, Saturday 29 and Sunday 30.

Friday 21, Saturday 22 and Sunday 23 August, then Friday 28, Saturday 29 and Sunday 30. Times Friday and Saturday at 8pm; Sunday matinees at 5pm.

Friday and Saturday at 8pm; Sunday matinees at 5pm. Free, but you must book Tickets cost nothing. Booking for the first weekend opened online at noon today; the second weekend opens at noon on Wednesday 26.

Tickets cost nothing. Booking for the first weekend opened online at noon today; the second weekend opens at noon on Wednesday 26. Two deadlines Online booking closes at noon on the day of each performance, and your reservation lapses twenty minutes before curtain-up.

Online booking closes at noon on the day of each performance, and your reservation lapses twenty minutes before curtain-up. The venue Sala Alberto Ginastera at the Teatro Argentino, Avenida 51 between 9 and 10, in the centre of La Plata. It seats about 2,000.

Sala Alberto Ginastera at the Teatro Argentino, Avenida 51 between 9 and 10, in the centre of La Plata. It seats about 2,000. Who is behind it Carlos Vieu conducts; María Jaunarena directs and designed the costumes; Gonzalo Córdova did the sets and lighting.

Carlos Vieu conducts; María Jaunarena directs and designed the costumes; Gonzalo Córdova did the sets and lighting. Full forces The Orquesta Estable, the Coro Estable and a children’s choir, with a double cast across the six nights. It runs 165 minutes.

A full orchestra, two choirs and one of the best-loved operas ever written — and the tickets cost nothing.

An hour from Buenos Aires there is a vast brutalist opera house that calls its main hall one of the most important in Latin America, and for two weekends in August it is staging The Magic Flute in La Plata for nothing. Not a reduced version, not a piano rehearsal — a full new production with orchestra, two choirs and a double cast. You just have to book online, and the window for the first three nights opened at midday today.

The Teatro Argentino’s Orquesta Estable plays all six performances. Admission is free. (Photo internet reproduction)

The Magic Flute in La Plata: the six dates, and how booking works

The run is split across two weekends. The first is Friday 21 August at 8pm, Saturday 22 August at 8pm and Sunday 23 August at 5pm. The second is Friday 28 and Saturday 29 August at 8pm, and Sunday 30 August at 5pm.

Reservations are made through the Teatro Argentino website and are released in two batches, both at noon: today for the opening weekend, Wednesday 26 August for the closing one. They go quickly, because free opera in Argentina always does. Over-65s and holders of a disability certificate can also reserve in person at the box office between noon and 6pm on those two days, with ID.

Two rules catch people out. Online booking shuts at noon on the day of the performance — you cannot decide at four o’clock to go that night. And your reservation only holds until twenty minutes before curtain-up, so arriving at 7.45pm for an 8pm start may mean your seat has gone. Aim to be inside by 7.30pm.

Who is singing

There are two casts, alternating across the six nights. Tamino, the prince, is sung by Darío Schmunck on 21, 23 and 29 August and by Santiago Martínez on 22, 28 and 30. Pamina alternates between Marisú Pavón and Ayelén Isaia; Papageno, the bird-catcher who gets most of the laughs, between Sebastián Sorarrain and Gabriel Carasso.

The Queen of the Night — the role with the aria everyone recognises, all stratospheric high notes and fury — is shared by María Gerk and Martina Gioiosa. Sarastro, the bass part at the other end of the range, alternates between Sebastián Barboza and Leonardo Palma.

Carlos Vieu conducts the Orquesta Estable. The Coro Estable is prepared by Santiago Cano and the Coro de Niñxs by Mónica Dagorret. María Jaunarena directs and designed the costumes, with sets and lighting by Gonzalo Córdova. The whole thing runs about 165 minutes.

Getting there from Buenos Aires

La Plata is about 60 kilometres south-east of the capital. The Roca line train from Constitución takes roughly an hour and a quarter and costs ARS 729 (about US$0.48) with a registered SUBE card, or a flat ARS 1,500 (about US$0.99) without one — which is what most visitors end up paying. City buses 129 and 195 also run, but at roughly ARS 4,800 (about US$3.17) they cost six times as much. By car on the Autopista it is about an hour outside rush hour.

The theatre is at Avenida 51 between 9 and 10, in the middle of La Plata’s grid, and the streets around it have plenty of places to eat before an 8pm start. For the Sunday matinees at 5pm you can comfortably make it there and back in an afternoon.

One warning about the building itself: the Teatro Argentino is a vast concrete complex and the Sala Ginastera is not the first room you walk into. Give yourself ten minutes to find it.

Why bother, if you have never been to an opera

The Magic Flute is the one to start with. It was written to be popular rather than grand — a fairy tale with a dragon, a bird-catcher in feathers, a wicked queen and jokes. The story is simple enough to follow from the staging alone. The theatre has not published which language this production is sung in, so check when you book if that matters to you.

And the price removes the last excuse. Opera has a reputation in most countries as a thing you save up for. In Argentina a good deal of it is publicly funded and genuinely free, which is one of the quieter pleasures of living here. If it turns out not to be for you, you have lost a dollar on the train.

Frequently Asked Questions

When are the performances of The Magic Flute in La Plata? There are six: Friday 21 August at 8pm, Saturday 22 August at 8pm, Sunday 23 August at 5pm, Friday 28 August at 8pm, Saturday 29 August at 8pm and Sunday 30 August at 5pm, all in the Sala Alberto Ginastera of the Teatro Argentino. Are the tickets really free, and how do I get them? Yes, admission is free. Tickets are reserved online through the Teatro Argentino website, released at noon in two batches — on Wednesday 19 August for the first weekend and Wednesday 26 August for the second. Online booking then closes at noon on the day of each performance, and a reservation lapses twenty minutes before curtain-up, so arrive early. Who is conducting and directing? Carlos Vieu conducts the Orquesta Estable. María Jaunarena directs the production and designed the costumes, with sets and lighting by Gonzalo Córdova. The Coro Estable is prepared by Santiago Cano and the Coro de Niñxs by Mónica Dagorret. The performance runs about 165 minutes. How do I get to La Plata from Buenos Aires? The Roca line train from Constitución takes about an hour and a quarter and costs ARS 729 (about US$0.48) with a registered SUBE card, or ARS 1,500 (about US$0.99) without one. Buses 129 and 195 make the trip for around ARS 4,800 (about US$3.17). By car the Autopista Buenos Aires-La Plata takes roughly an hour outside peak times. The theatre is at Avenida 51 between 9 and 10.

World.title: What Is Free in Quito This Week, Balloons Included
World.content:
Ecuador · Culture

Key Facts Free balloons in town On Thursday 20 August the festival’s Noche de las Luces comes into Quito for the first time, free, at three sites at once.

On Thursday 20 August the festival’s Noche de las Luces comes into Quito for the first time, free, at three sites at once. Thursday in La Mariscal Los Jueves de Agosto runs Thursday 20 August from 5pm to about 9pm across the neighbourhood. Most of it is free; anything that is not is priced in the programme.

Los Jueves de Agosto runs Thursday 20 August from 5pm to about 9pm across the neighbourhood. Most of it is free; anything that is not is priced in the programme. One paid extra The guided La Mariscal Creativa route costs US$5 a head, starts at 5pm at Café Qinti, and needs booking at visitquito.ec.

The guided La Mariscal Creativa route costs US$5 a head, starts at 5pm at Café Qinti, and needs booking at visitquito.ec. Free cinema “Te falta calle: La puerta de los sueños” screens free at the Cinemateca Nacional, Casa de la Cultura Ecuatoriana, at 6pm on Thursday 20 August.

“Te falta calle: La puerta de los sueños” screens free at the Cinemateca Nacional, Casa de la Cultura Ecuatoriana, at 6pm on Thursday 20 August. Already finished The Turicine festival ended on 15 August. If you see it in an August listing, the listing is out of date.

The Turicine festival ended on 15 August. If you see it in an August listing, the listing is out of date. Where to wander Café Qinti, Base Distrito Creativo, Casa Silberstein, Fundación Kingman, the Museo de Arte Naif and Quito Jazz Club are among the venues taking part.

Café Qinti, Base Distrito Creativo, Casa Silberstein, Fundación Kingman, the Museo de Arte Naif and Quito Jazz Club are among the venues taking part. The main event The Mitad del Mundo balloon festival runs 20 to 23 August, gates at 5am, flights 6am to 8am. Tickets are online only, and there are separate ones for the balloons and the concerts.

The balloon festival takes the photographs. But this year the balloons come to town for free, and that is only the start of the week.

Quito in August is busy in a way that can be misleading. The big balloon festival at Mitad del Mundo gets the attention and the crowds, and it is worth the early start — but it costs money and it is a trip out of town. What most people do not know is that this year the balloons also come into the city, for nothing, on Thursday night. Here are the free things to do in Quito between Thursday and Sunday — and the one thing worth paying for.

Quito’s historic centre. The balloon festival comes into the city free on Thursday night. (Photo internet reproduction)

Thursday night in La Mariscal

La Mariscal spent years as the neighbourhood everyone warned you about after dark. The city has been working to change that, and Los Jueves de Agosto is the result: every Thursday this month, more than thirty activities across restaurants, galleries and cultural spaces, from 5pm to around 9pm.

The venues taking part include Café Qinti, the Base Distrito Creativo, Casa Silberstein, the Fundación Kingman, the Museo de Arte Naif Latinoamericano, CatFe Art, NÜA and the Quito Jazz Club. Most activities are free; the ones that are not are priced in the programme.

The one worth paying for is La Mariscal Creativa, a guided route through the neighbourhood’s creative spaces at US$5 a person. It starts at 5pm at Café Qinti, ends at the Base Distrito Creativo, covers the guide and coffee tastings, and must be booked in advance at visitquito.ec. For anyone new to Quito it is the cheapest orientation to a district you would otherwise avoid out of habit.

Free cinema at the Casa de la Cultura

The Cinemateca Nacional, inside the Casa de la Cultura Ecuatoriana, runs free screenings all month. On Thursday 20 August at 6pm it shows “Te falta calle: La puerta de los sueños”, Alex Chasiguano’s 2026 documentary, 61 minutes, programmed with the city’s San José foundation to mark the international day of struggle for people living on the street. The Casa de la Cultura has two cinemas, so check the board on arrival for the room.

A second free strand runs just outside the weekend: “Dos formas de mirar” pairs documentary with fiction on Tuesdays at 6pm in the Sala Augusto San Miguel, for the Cinemateca’s 45th anniversary. The next session is Tuesday 25 August.

The balloons, free and paid

The best-kept secret of the week is that on Thursday 20 August the festival’s Noche de las Luces leaves Mitad del Mundo and comes into the city for the first time, free of charge, running at three places at once: the Liga Barrial ground in Solanda, the Carapungo stadium and the Plaza de la República below the Pichincha prefecture. Tethered balloons, performances and photo spots, and nobody takes your money at the gate.

The main festival at Ciudad Mitad del Mundo runs 20 to 23 August. Gates open at 5am and the balloons fly between 6am and 8am only, so this is a genuine dawn start. Admission has been US$5 for adults and US$2.50 for children, over-65s and disabled visitors, and there are separate tickets for the morning balloons and the evening concerts — you need both to do both. Tickets are sold online, with no box office. Prices for this edition had not been restated when we published, so check the official portal before you set out.

Free things to do in Quito on a budget

Quito rewards people who look past the obvious. The historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage site you can walk for free, and the Casa de la Cultura programmes something most days.

The practical advice for anyone who has just arrived: the city sits at about 2,850 metres, which means evenings get cold quickly and a 5pm start feels later than it is. Take a jacket to a Thursday evening in La Mariscal, and do not plan a heavy day before a 5am start at Mitad del Mundo.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is free in Quito between 20 and 23 August 2026? The balloon festival’s Noche de las Luces on Thursday 20 August is free at three sites in the city — Solanda, Carapungo and the Plaza de la República. Most of Los Jueves de Agosto in La Mariscal that evening is free too, from about 5pm to 9pm, as are the Cinemateca Nacional screenings at the Casa de la Cultura Ecuatoriana, including “Te falta calle: La puerta de los sueños” at 6pm on Thursday. What is Los Jueves de Agosto? It is a city initiative running every Thursday in August in the La Mariscal district of Quito, with more than thirty activities in restaurants, galleries and cultural spaces from 5pm to around 9pm. Participating venues include Café Qinti, Base Distrito Creativo, Casa Silberstein, the Fundación Kingman and the Quito Jazz Club. Most activities are free and the priced ones are marked; the guided La Mariscal Creativa route costs US$5 and must be booked in advance at visitquito.ec. Is the Turicine festival still running? No. The seventh edition of the Ecuadorian Turicine festival ended on 15 August 2026, so it does not fall within this week despite appearing in some August listings. How much is the balloon festival? The Festival Internacional del Globo Mitad del Mundo runs from 20 to 23 August at Ciudad Mitad del Mundo, with gates at 5am and flights between 6am and 8am. Admission has been US$5 for adults and US$2.50 for children, visitors over 65 and disabled visitors, with separate tickets for the morning balloons and the evening concerts. Tickets are sold online only. Check the official portal for this edition’s prices before travelling.

World.title: Ten Days of Free Short Films in São Paulo, and How to Get a Seat
World.content:
Brazil · Cinema

Key Facts Free everywhere Every session of the 37th Curta Kinoforum is free, in seven cinemas across the city, from 20 to 30 August.

Every session of the 37th Curta Kinoforum is free, in seven cinemas across the city, from 20 to 30 August. Get there early At MIS, tickets are handed out at the box office one hour before each session. There is no online booking, and the room seats about 170.

At MIS, tickets are handed out at the box office one hour before each session. There is no online booking, and the room seats about 170. The dates The festival runs 20 to 30 August, after an opening night at CineSesc on 19 August.

This is the 37th Curta Kinoforum, one of the oldest short-film festivals in Latin America. The numbers 260 films from 58 countries — 127 Brazilian, 133 foreign — including an international selection of 109 films from 55 countries.

260 films from 58 countries — 127 Brazilian, 133 foreign — including an international selection of 109 films from 55 countries. Something for children MIS runs Kids sessions on 23 August at 2pm, and two on 30 August, at 10.30am and noon.

Ten days of short films, none of them longer than your lunch break, and not one of them costs anything.

Short films are the easiest cinema to watch in a language you are still learning. Nothing lasts long, the story is usually told with pictures rather than dialogue, and if one does not work there is another along in four minutes. From Thursday there are free short films in São Paulo by the hundred — 260 of them, to be exact.

Where to see free short films in São Paulo

The Museu da Imagem e do Som is one of seven cinemas in this year’s Curta Kinoforum, and it is the one worth building an evening around. Its share of the programme is the Brazilian selection — the Mostra Brasil blocks, numbered one to twelve — plus the children’s sessions and the closing best-of. It screens on 20, 21, 22, 23, 25, 26, 27, 29 and 30 August, and is dark on the 24th and 28th.

Most evenings run two sessions, at 6pm and 8pm. On 25 August there are two Diálogos Urbanos sessions, one on São Paulo and one on Recife, which is as good an introduction to how Brazilians film their own cities as you will get in one night.

The closing weekend is the strongest. On 29 and 30 August MIS shows the 10+ blocks — ten Brazilian and ten foreign — plus a Destaques session of the festival’s highlights.

How to actually get in

This is the part people get wrong. Entry is free, but there is no online reservation and no advance booking. Tickets are released at the MIS box office one hour before each session, and popular blocks do fill.

So for a 6pm session, be at Avenida Europa 158 by 5pm. The room seats about 170, so the queue is real. On most evenings there is a second block two hours later, though on 22 and 23 August the 6pm session is the last one.

If you are bringing children, the Kids sessions are on 23 August at 2pm and 30 August at 10.30am and noon. The 30 August morning slot is billed as a marathon, which in practice means a long, cheerful, sit-down-and-stay session.

The rest of the festival

The full 37th Kinoforum is much larger: 260 films from 58 countries across the Cinemateca Brasileira, CineSesc, the Spcine circuit at the Centro Cultural São Paulo, Espaço Petrobras de Cinema, MIS and the two CINUSP rooms. Of those, 109 films from 55 countries make up the international selection — which is where to go if you want the view from outside Brazil. The opening was at CineSesc on 19 August at 8pm.

If you cannot get to a cinema, part of the programme streams free on Spcine Play, Porta Curtas, Itaú Cultural Play and Sesc Digital — useful if you are outside São Paulo, or outside Brazil.

Why this is worth your Thursday

If you have moved to Brazil recently, the cost of going out is the thing that surprises people most. A cinema ticket in São Paulo typically runs from about R$30 to R$60 (about US$6 to US$12), and a festival night elsewhere in the world would cost several times that. This costs nothing at all.

It is also a low-effort way to understand where you now live. Twelve blocks of Brazilian shorts is twelve blocks of Brazilians describing their own country to each other, without the filter of an export market. You will learn more in two hours there than in a month of news.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the short film festival in São Paulo free? Yes. Every session of the 37th Curta Kinoforum is free, in every venue, and part of the programme also streams free online. There is no advance booking at MIS: tickets are handed out at the box office one hour before each session, on a first-come basis. How many films are showing and where? The 37th Curta Kinoforum shows 260 films from 58 countries — 127 Brazilian and 133 foreign — of which 109 films from 55 countries form the international selection. They screen across seven cinemas: MIS, the Cinemateca Brasileira, CineSesc, the Spcine room at the Centro Cultural São Paulo, Espaço Petrobras de Cinema and the two CINUSP rooms. MIS carries the Brazilian selection. Where is MIS and how do I get there? The Museu da Imagem e do Som is at Avenida Europa 158, Jardim Europa, in the west of São Paulo. It is a short taxi or ride-hailing trip from Avenida Paulista; the nearest metro stations are a walk away, so most people arrive by car or app. Allow an hour before your session to collect a ticket. Are the films subtitled? Foreign films are subtitled in Portuguese, and every in-person session carries Portuguese subtitles for the deaf and hard of hearing, so Brazilian films are subtitled too — which many language learners find useful. Short films lean heavily on images, so the barrier is lower than at a feature-film festival.

World.content:
Mexico · Books

Key Facts The dates The 34th FIL Monterrey runs from 10 to 18 October at Cintermex, the convention centre in Parque Fundidora.

The 34th FIL Monterrey runs from 10 to 18 October at Cintermex, the convention centre in Parque Fundidora. Entry is free There is no admission charge for the fair, which is unusual for an event of this size in Mexico.

There is no admission charge for the fair, which is unusual for an event of this size in Mexico. A Nobel winner Jean-Marie Gustave Le Clézio, the 2008 Nobel laureate, comes to present his book on Mexico.

Jean-Marie Gustave Le Clézio, the 2008 Nobel laureate, comes to present his book on Mexico. Cuba’s best-known novelist Leonardo Padura, creator of the Havana detective Mario Conde, is also confirmed.

The Pabellón de la Niñez runs on the theme of air this year, with 990 sessions and 61 performances. Who runs it The fair is organised by the Tecnológico de Monterrey, and school groups can register from 1 September.

A Nobel laureate, the man who reinvented the Cuban detective novel, and not a peso to get in.

If you live in northern Mexico, or you are the kind of person who plans a trip around a bookshop, put 10 to 18 October in your calendar now. FIL Monterrey 2026 has published its line-up, and it is a strong one: a Nobel laureate, a Cuban novelist with a worldwide readership, and free entry for all nine days.

Monterrey. The city’s 34th international book fair runs 10–18 October at Cintermex, free. (Photo internet reproduction)

Who is coming to FIL Monterrey 2026

The headline name is Jean-Marie Gustave Le Clézio, the French writer who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2008 and who has spent much of his life writing about Mexico. He comes to present Tres entradas a México. He is joined by Emmanuel Carrère, the French author whose non-fiction reads like a thriller, and by Leonardo Padura from Cuba, whose Mario Conde novels are the closest thing Latin American crime fiction has to a household name.

From the United States comes the poet Rita Dove, a former Poet Laureate and Pulitzer winner. From Argentina and Canada, Alberto Manguel, who gives the opening address. From Denmark, Janne Teller; from Chile, Lina Meruane. And from Mexico itself, a strong domestic bench: Cristina Rivera Garza, Juan Villoro, Enrique Krauze, the composer Gabriela Ortiz, the archaeologists Eduardo Matos Moctezuma and Leonardo López Luján, and the jurist José Ramón Cossío.

Gioconda Belli, the Nicaraguan poet and novelist, completes a list that is unusually international for a regional fair.

What else is on

Beyond the author talks, the fair runs a Congress on Children’s and Young Adult Literature and meetings for reading promoters and librarians. New this year is a philosophy strand, Sentir y pensar nuestro tiempo, with Darío Sztajnszrajber, Mujica, Quintana and Campos Salvaterra — philosophy staged as public conversation rather than lecture.

For families there are two separate strands. The Pabellón de la Niñez takes air as its 2026 theme, with 990 sessions and 61 performances for younger children. The Programa Juvenil, for secondary and preparatory age, handles reading, mental health, critical thinking and the environment. Entry to the fair is free; a handful of literary workshops charge.

The practical part

Cintermex, in Parque Fundidora on the east side of Monterrey, is the main venue — a large, well-signposted convention centre with parking, and the park around it is one of the better places in the city to spend an afternoon either side of a session. A few sessions run off-site: the screening of Iñárritu’s entry speech to El Colegio Nacional is at CONARTE’s Cineteca on 13 October, and a documentary shows at MARCO on 16 October.

Entry is free, so the constraint is not money but seating. Popular author talks at Mexican book fairs fill early, and the pattern at Cintermex is the usual one: arrive twenty minutes before a big name, or watch from the back.

October in Monterrey is pleasant — warm days, cool evenings, none of the summer heat that makes the city hard work in July. If you have been meaning to visit and have not, this is the week.

Why a book fair matters here

Mexico’s book fairs are not quiet trade events. FIL Guadalajara is the largest Spanish-language book fair in the world, and Monterrey’s — run by the Tecnológico de Monterrey and now in its 34th year — works as its northern cousin: less overwhelming, easier to navigate, and free.

For anyone living in Latin America and reading in Spanish — or trying to — a fair like this is the cheapest way to fill a shelf. Publishers discount heavily on the floor, small presses you will never see in a chain bookshop take stands, and the authors are in the room rather than on a screen. Nine days, no ticket, and you can go back as often as you like.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is FIL Monterrey 2026 and where? The 34th FIL Monterrey runs from 10 to 18 October 2026 at Cintermex, the convention centre in Parque Fundidora on the eastern side of Monterrey, Nuevo León. A few sessions take place off-site at CONARTE’s Cineteca and at the MARCO museum. Does FIL Monterrey cost anything? Entry to the fair is free for all nine days. Books are of course sold on the floor, and publishers typically discount there. A handful of literary workshops are listed as paid events, but the fair itself and the author sessions carry no admission charge. Which authors are confirmed? Announced guests include the Nobel laureate Jean-Marie Gustave Le Clézio, Emmanuel Carrère, Leonardo Padura, Rita Dove, Alberto Manguel, Gioconda Belli, Janne Teller, Lina Meruane, Cristina Rivera Garza, Juan Villoro, Enrique Krauze, Gabriela Ortiz, Eduardo Matos Moctezuma, Leonardo López Luján and José Ramón Cossío. Manguel gives the inaugural address. Is there anything for children? Yes. The Pabellón de la Niñez takes air as its 2026 theme, with 990 sessions and 61 performances for younger children, while the Programa Juvenil covers reading, mental health, critical thinking and the environment for teenagers. There is also a Congress on Children’s and Young Adult Literature. School groups can register from 1 September.

World.title: Costa Rica Closes Turrialba Volcano and Guayabo Monument Due to Heavy Rains
World.content:
Two popular to visit in the Turrialba area have closed temporarily as continued rainfall and saturated ground raise the risk of landslides and other emergencies. The public areas of Turrialba Volcano National Park and Guayabo National Monument closed today and will remain off-limits until further notice. The measure goes for tourists, guides and government personnel working at both sites.

The National System of Conservation Areas said the closure responds to unstable weather conditions and the orange alert in effect for the canton of Turrialba. Officials will reassess both sites once the emergency period ends before deciding whether visitors can safely return. The decision is tied to the weather rather than a change in volcanic activity at Turrialba Volcano.

Authorities said the purpose is to prevent people from entering areas where heavy rain may have weakened the ground, affected trails or increased the possibility of falling material. Visitors should not attempt to enter either protected area while the closure remains in place. Tour operators and travelers with planned visits are being advised to check official updates before traveling to the area.

Guayabo National Monument protects Costa Rica’s most important pre-Columbian archaeological site. Its stone roads, aqueducts, foundations and ceremonial structures offer a look at a settlement that flourished centuries before the arrival of Europeans. Turrialba Volcano National Park, meanwhile, gives visitors access to one of the best-known active volcanoes here in Costa Rica.

The park’s location and elevation also make it particularly exposed to rapidly changing weather, strong winds and difficult trail conditions. The closures come as Costa Rica continues dealing with the effects of consecutive tropical waves. More than 1,300 people remained in emergency shelters Tuesday, while authorities delivered assistance to isolated communities in the Caribbean and mountainous Indigenous territories.

Heavy rainfall has also caused flooding, landslides and repeated road closures. Although conditions improved in some locations Tuesday, emergency officials warned that saturated soil could continue producing incidents even when rainfall temporarily decreases. SINAC will determine when Turrialba Volcano National Park and Guayabo National Monument can reopen after reviewing conditions and receiving updated guidance from emergency officials. No reopening date had been announced as of yet.

World.title: BEL implements COPA adjustment of 1.5 cents per kWh for August
World.content:
BEL implements COPA adjustment of 1.5 cents per kWh for August

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belize Electricity Limited (BEL) has announced the implementation of a Cost of Power Adjustment (COPA) mechanism effective August 2026, following the Public Utilities Commission’s (PUC) final decision in the 2026/2027 Annual Review Proceeding.

Under the decision, the PUC established a Regulatory Sandbox to evaluate and apply COPA on a month-to-month basis.

For August 2026, the regulator approved an adjustment of 1.5 cents per kilowatt-hour (kWh), which will be applied to customers’ August electricity bills.

BEL said the actual cost of power over the past six months was 4.3 cents per kWh higher than the reference cost approved by the PUC.

However, the Regulatory Sandbox limits any monthly COPA adjustment to a maximum of 1.5 cents per kWh, providing customers with protection against sudden and significant changes in electricity costs.

The company explained that future monthly adjustments could increase, decrease, result in a rebate, or remain at zero, depending on the actual cost of power and the PUC’s approval each month.

BEL will submit verified operational and financial data to the regulator for monthly review, with approved COPA adjustments appearing as a separate line item on customers’ bills.

World.title: Ministry of E-Governance hands over VEX V5 Classroom Super Robotics Kit to University of Belize
World.content:
Ministry of E-Governance hands over VEX V5 Classroom Super Robotics Kit to University of Belize

By Zoila Palma: On August 18, 2026, the Ministry of E-Governance handed over a VEX V5 Classroom Super Robotics Kit to the University of Belize.

The donation supports the university’s Jaguar Tech Studio, an initiative dedicated to advancing student learning and innovation in robotics and technology.

The VEX V5 Classroom Super Kit is a comprehensive educational robotics platform featuring more than 1,500 components, including a Robot Brain, Controller, Smart Motors, a rechargeable battery and charger, sensors, and a wide range of structural and mechanical parts. With access to this technology, students can move beyond theoretical concepts and gain hands-on experience designing, building, programming, testing, and refining robotic systems.

The Ministry says that this partnership with UB reflects its continued commitment to advancing digital transformation and strengthening digital skills across Belize, in alignment with the priorities of the National Digital Agenda.

“As technology continues to reshape industries and the future of work, building practical competencies in areas such as programming, automation, robotics, and artificial intelligence will be essential to Belize’s continued growth and competitiveness,” the Ministry said.

The Ministry will also be strategically donating additional robotics kits to other organizations and educational institutions across the country, helping to expand access to emerging technologies and create more opportunities for Belizeans to develop the digital skills needed for the future.
