The plans go beyond container shipping. Proposed electricity and digital cable projects across the Caspian would also bring energy and information flows into the broader agenda of regional cooperation.

The route through Nakhchivan offers new opportunities but remains contentious. The Washington Declaration, signed on 8 August 2025, provides for a transport link through Armenia between mainland Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan, based on the sovereignty and jurisdiction of the states concerned, as well as the development of the TRIPP mechanism. Baku calls the route the “Zangezur Corridor”.

If implemented, the route could give the Middle Corridor an additional link to Turkey. However, until the parties agree on customs procedures, security arrangements, financing and management mechanisms, it remains a project rather than an operational transport corridor.

What is changing from a geopolitical perspective?

“C6” is a convenient political label, not the official name of an organisation. The format remains a consultative platform based on consensus. It does not involve collective defence commitments or mechanisms to enforce decisions.

For Moscow, this is therefore primarily about competition over logistics and political influence, including through the development of routes that bypass Russia, rather than the emergence of a new military alliance.

Beijing gains an additional route to the west and more stable conditions for transit.

Ankara has an interest in strengthening direct transport links across the Caspian.

The European Union and the US see the format as an opportunity to reduce dependence on routes through Russia and expand access to Central Asia.

The new C6 format should not be confused with the Organisation of Turkic States. The OTS has a treaty-based framework and institutional cooperation among Turkic states. The “Central Asia and Azerbaijan” format also includes Tajikistan and focuses less on shared identity than on geography, economic interests and regional cooperation.

Potential opportunities and real constraints

The potential areas for cooperation are quite concrete: common transit tariffs, digital customs procedures, coordinated port and railway schedules, joint investment funds, green energy exports, tourism routes and coordination at international forums. With its ports, financial resources and transport links through the Caucasus and Turkey, Azerbaijan offers Central Asian countries additional routes and opportunities. Baku, in turn, gains more systematic access to the region’s five markets and their economic ties with China.

However, there are also many constraints. The six countries differ in their economic potential, interests in water resources and energy, and priorities in their relations with Russia, China, Turkey and the West. The format has no permanent secretariat or mechanisms to enforce decisions, so implementation of political agreements will depend on intergovernmental coordination.

The Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea, signed in 2018, has yet to be ratified by Iran, while delimiting the seabed requires separate agreements. Falling water levels in the Caspian, the shallowing of ports and the need for costly dredging also increase the environmental and economic costs of transport logistics.

From symbol to concrete projects?

Mirziyoyev has already proposed transforming the format into a “Community of Central Asia” with a rotating secretariat. The next official meeting, scheduled for 8 October 2026 in Avaza, will be one of the first tests of whether these intentions can turn into practical decisions.

Will the six countries agree on common tariffs, digital customs procedures and a stable ferry schedule? Will TRIPP become a fully fledged part of the Middle Corridor without creating new border disputes? Or will the “Central Asia and Azerbaijan” format remain a flexible consultative platform, with its informal nature continuing to be its main advantage?

Azerbaijan at Central Asia’s table

World.title: Convicted former Georgian PM Garibashvili: ‘Authorities left me no choice, I have to fight’
World.content:
Letter from Georgia’s former prime minister from prison

Convicted former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili says in a letter published from prison that the authorities arrested him to end his political career. He also says he gave up his legal fight to avoid a confrontation with the authorities.

The former prime minister writes that he received a letter from Regional Development Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze in July. According to Garibashvili, he confirmed to Mdinaradze that same day that he did not intend to return to politics.

Mamuka Mdinaradze’s press office has described Garibashvili’s claims as “complete absurdity”.

“I state with full responsibility that I did everything to avoid confrontation with the [ruling] team and with someone who is dear to me,” Garibashvili wrote.

He says this is why he abandoned his legal challenge and went through the entire process to the end — to avoid, as he put it, harming the interests of the state and the “team”.

“Unfortunately, in response I received a staged dirty provocation, a sea of lies and injustice. Throughout this time, the public heard not a single word from me. I endured this ordeal patiently,” Garibashvili said.

According to Garibashvili, despite the position he had expressed to Mdinaradze, the authorities believed there was still a “1% risk” that he might return to politics in the future.

“To avoid this, they wanted me to face corruption charges and admit guilt,” Garibashvili writes.

According to him, this demand became a “red line” that forced him to take the “most difficult step of my life” — to turn against the authorities.

“I have no other choice. I am forced to start fighting,” the former prime minister said.

On 17 August 2026, Garibashvili made his first public statement from prison. In a Facebook post, he said he had received an ultimatum in a letter sent on the instructions of Bidzina Ivanishvili. He added that he had “no other choice” but to stand against what he described as “evil that insults my dignity”.

“I tried to do everything possible to avoid taking this step, but unfortunately I have no other choice but to confront this evil that insults my dignity. I must confront this ruthless cruelty, oppression and injustice, as well as the dirty plan to destroy me and my family,” Garibashvili wrote.

He also said that Bidzina Ivanishvili and the government bear responsibility for the safety of both himself and his family.

In the letter, Garibashvili says he had remained publicly silent and patiently endured what was happening until now. However, he says the current situation has left him no choice but to begin fighting.

Letter from Georgia’s former prime minister from prison

World.title: Armenian prime minister’s wife launches campaign against domestic violence
World.content:
Anna Hakobyan’s campaign against domestic violence

The wife of Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, Anna Hakobyan, has announced the launch of a campaign against domestic violence. She received death threats shortly after calling for a public discussion of the issue. However, she continues to actively promote her initiative.

“The first stage will involve drafting comprehensive and effective legislation and discussing it in the National Assembly,” she said.

According to Anna Hakobyan, the Criminal Code should define domestic violence separately as “a distinct and independent crime”. She plans to invite female MPs from the parliament’s two opposition factions to join her initiative. If they do, she believes there is a chance that “parliament will unanimously approve the bill”.

Anna Hakobyan calls for a “family model with no place for violence”

The prime minister’s wife posted a video message on social media in which she said she intended to continue fighting domestic violence. According to Hakobyan, Armenia’s traditional family model, which hides various forms of violence, should give way to a model of a “family with no place for violence, based on mutual love and respect”. She proposes amending the Criminal Code to achieve this goal:

“An individual article should be added to the Code to establish criminal liability for all forms of domestic violence. Alternatively, different chapters of the Code could include provisions covering specific forms of domestic violence, including beatings, psychological abuse, economic abuse, bodily harm, sexual violence and others.”

According to Anna Hakobyan, eradicating violence requires clear, realistic and effective legal mechanisms.

Before presenting the bill to parliament, she initiated discussions with independent experts and female MPs. Together, they plan to examine gaps in the existing legislation. Once the law comes into force, she has promised to launch the initiative’s second stage. This will involve:

organising an awareness campaign;

improving the skills of staff at relevant agencies;

ensuring the effective implementation of the new regulations.

“At the same time, a group of respected experts is preparing a nationwide study to collect the most accurate and comprehensive data possible on the prevalence of domestic violence against women in Armenia,” she said.

What preceded the campaign

This is not the prime minister’s wife’s first post about domestic violence. She has been actively raising the issue on her social media pages. At the end of July, she said she had received threats after a particular post, including threats to kill her.

“I hope the state authorities can prevent such a development, as it would seriously damage the country’s reputation if the prime minister’s wife became a victim of violence,” Hakobyan said.

At the same time, she urged women to overcome their fears and report cases of violence.

The Prosecutor General’s Office took note of her report. The Investigative Committee said it had opened a criminal case under the article on “hooliganism using information and communication technologies”.

“In addition, within the framework of another criminal case concerning public calls for violence, a warrant has been issued for the arrest of one person. The person has been placed on the wanted list,” Investigative Committee spokeswoman Kim Avdalyan said.

Statistics on domestic violence

The Investigative Committee said it opened 1,794 criminal cases related to domestic violence in the first half of 2026:

712 cases carried over from 2025;

1,082 cases opened in 2026.

Authorities sent 204 criminal cases to court and charged 213 people.

Of the 213 defendants in the cases sent to court, 150 were spouses of the victims, 20 were partners, 15 were parents or grandparents, five were brothers or sisters, 16 were children or grandchildren, one was the husband’s sister or brother, and six were sons- or daughters-in-law.

Of the 213 victims, 192 were over 18, while the rest were minors. Of those, 13 were under 12, three were aged 13-14, and five were aged 15-18.

Anna Hakobyan’s campaign against domestic violence

World.title: ‘Work is being carried out to international standards’ — Georgia’s Gelati Monastery Rehabilitation Committee responds to criticism
World.content:
Restoration of Georgia’s Gelati Monastery

The Temporary Committee for the Rehabilitation of Gelati has described reports circulating on social media and in the media about conservation work at the monastery as disinformation.

The committee said the disinformation was harming efforts to restore Gelati.

The Gelati Monastery complex is one of Georgia’s most important medieval cultural and religious monuments. King David IV, known as David the Builder, founded it in 1106.

The complex’s main church is the Cathedral of the Nativity of the Virgin Mary. In medieval Georgia, Gelati was not only a monastery but also an important centre of education and scholarship, home to the renowned Gelati Academy.

Recent reports and assessments have raised concerns about the condition of Gelati. The debate has focused on several issues:

The church’s temporary roof, which critics have called “cellophane”;

The risk of frescoes collapsing;

Mould and condensation inside the church;

The condition of the drainage system;

Plans to install an underfloor heating system;

Cooperation with the Italian institute Opificio delle Pietre Dure;

The condition of the mosaics at Gelati.

What does the committee say?

The committee rejects claims that the Gelati Cathedral is covered with “cellophane”. According to the committee, the creation of a single temporary covering for the cathedral was one of the main requirements set by the UNESCO World Heritage Centre as early as 2020.

The committee says Georgian and German specialists jointly designed the roof. The authorities approved the project after considering several proposals. The covering uses a high-tech PVC-based material made in Germany specifically for Gelati. According to the committee, the material meets international conservation standards.

The committee also rejects reports of widespread loss of frescoes inside the cathedral. It says all critically damaged areas have been stabilised, while conservation work on the wall paintings is continuing in stages.

The statement also addresses Gelati’s historic drainage system. According to the committee, drainage channels built during the reign of David the Builder stopped functioning in 1510 after Ottoman forces burned the monastery. The committee says archaeological excavations also support this conclusion.

“For centuries, the drainage system was filled with earth, ash and coal,” the committee said.

The committee also responded to criticism over humidity and condensation inside the church. According to the committee, Italian professor Dario Camuffo conducted the study of Gelati’s microclimate. The committee considers him one of the recognised experts in the study of the microclimate of cultural heritage sites.

The committee explained that the problem at Gelati stems from the church’s massive walls, which retain the cold for a long time during winter. In spring, when outdoor temperatures rise and warm air enters the church, condensation can form on the walls and floor.

Camuffo suggested gradually heating the floor as one possible solution. However, the committee stressed that this remains a working hypothesis and requires further research before a final decision.

The committee also clarified the memorandum it signed with the Italian institute Opificio delle Pietre Dure. According to the committee, the “pilot restoration” provided for in the document does not mean conducting experiments at Gelati. Instead, it refers to pilot or trial restoration work, which is standard international practice.

“This is a widely accepted standard for restoring wall paintings. Before treating an entire fresco, conservators test the safety of the proposed conservation methods on a small, less visible area. Only after obtaining a positive result do they begin the full-scale process,” the committee said.

In a significant part of its statement, the committee also responded to critics and addressed allegations about the condition of the mosaics at Gelati.

According to the committee, experts already knew about the poor condition of the mosaics in 1989. The claim is based on an assessment by restorer Carlo Bakuradze at the time, who found that about 85% of the mosaic depicting the Virgin Mary had detached from its base.

The committee also criticised specialists who question the ongoing conservation work and reminded them of their own responsibility for Gelati’s condition in the past.

“It is cynical and hypocritical for people to question the quality of conservation work when, under their direct supervision, extensive water-infiltration problems emerged within just one year at the recently built Bagrati Cathedral — problems that persist to this day,” the statement said. The Temporary Committee for the Rehabilitation of Gelati urged critics not to try to damage the reputation of the ongoing work and to act according to professional ethics.

“We call on those pursuing certain subjective goals and agendas to refrain from attempts to discredit the conservation work carried out under the Gelati rehabilitation programme and deliberately mislead the public. We also call on them to return to the standards of common decency and professional ethics,” the committee said.

The committee concluded by stressing again that the work at the Gelati Monastery complex is unprecedented in scale, involves international experts and meets international conservation standards.

What happened at Gelati?

The main problem at Gelati Monastery is water and dampness, which have damaged the church’s wall paintings and mosaics over time. The situation became particularly serious after restoration work in recent years, including problems with the roof.

The problem became so serious that the UNESCO World Heritage Centre and its advisory bodies issued specific recommendations to Georgia. The authorities changed their approach to the restoration work in response to those recommendations and established the current Rehabilitation Committee.

A ruling by Georgia’s Supreme Court also notes that workers carried out roofing work at Gelati without an adequate expert assessment. The court found that problems with the materials used and the quality of the installation created a real risk of water entering the building.

Restoration of Georgia’s Gelati Monastery

World.title: Suicides in Armenia’s military: the statistics and debate over who should be held responsible
World.content:
Suicides in Armenia’s army: statistics

In Armenia, debate continues over the causes of military deaths in peacetime and who should bear responsibility. A series of suicides has prompted the latest discussions. The first incident occurred on 21 July. Then, on 13 August, the Defence Ministry reported that it had found the body of serviceman Grigor Zakaryan with a gunshot wound. In both cases, the Investigative Committee said it had opened criminal proceedings under the article on negligent incitement to suicide.

According to the Vanadzor office of the Helsinki Citizens’ Assembly, this was the 31st military death in Armenia in 2026. However, the Defence Ministry says 11 servicemen have died. Moreover, the ministry’s spokesperson said the number of military deaths had become the subject of various forms of manipulation.

“We often see reports in the press about 30 deaths in the army over the course of a year. But no one says how many of those 30 cases actually occurred in the army, which were related to military service and which were not. Even if the deaths were related to service, were all of them murders and suicides?” Aram Torosyan said, calling for greater precision.

Government bodies and civil society organisations also differ over who should bear responsibility for military deaths. Human rights groups tend to argue that the defence minister and the chief of the General Staff should be held accountable. However, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan does not share this view.

“In my assessment, it is not the case that the chief of the General Staff and the defence minister are failing to make sufficient efforts to address this issue,” Nikol Pashinyan said.

Civil society data differs from official figures

Human rights activist Nazeli Movsesyan, who represents the Vanadzor office of the Helsinki Citizens’ Assembly, said she had seen no positive changes. According to her, the number of military deaths in non-combat situations has not decreased:

“The situation is even worse than in 2025. There were 35 deaths throughout 2025, while there have already been 31 cases in the first eight months of this year.”

She stressed that 10 cases in 2025 were classified as related to military service, while the same number have been recorded in just eight months this year.

Defence Ministry spokesman Aram Torosyan says these claims do not match the official statistics.

“We have recorded 11 deaths this year. Only five of those who died were serving their mandatory military service. Some died from illness, while others died in a mine explosion,” he said.

Torosyan said six of the 11 deaths involved suicide or incitement to suicide, but only three were related to military service.

Commenting on last year’s figures, he stressed that there were no cases of murder in the army in 2025.

Causes of suicides in the army

The authorities have not released details about the death of serviceman Grigor Zakaryan. However, the prime minister said that 85-90% of suicides in the army result from:

gambling addiction and the debts it causes;

personal and family problems;

servicemen falling asleep while on duty, which can lead to conflicts with fellow soldiers.

“If a serviceman on duty at a border post falls asleep, he puts other people’s lives at risk. Soldiers then begin to treat the person who fell asleep at the post negatively, and he becomes isolated. After returning from combat duty, psychological pressure can also follow. We should not place all the blame on the army leadership. I am responsible for the fact that we have still not found a solution to this problem,” Pashinyan said.

Human rights activist Nazeli Movsesyan believes that the first two causes mentioned by the prime minister have nothing to do with the army. At the same time, she believes authorities can eliminate the third factor by taking systemic measures:

“Why does a serviceman fall asleep while on duty? Are there enough personnel to ensure that everyone gets enough rest and does not feel the need to sleep while on duty?”

Prime minister’s statements and dismissals

On the day the soldier died, Nikol Pashinyan told reporters that the government had discussed the situation and decided to make dismissals. He announced personnel changes in the Military Police and the Defence Ministry’s Department of Moral and Psychological Support:

“We will analyse in detail why our efforts in this area are not producing the desired results and draw conclusions. Yes, there must be individual accountability.”

The same day, reports emerged that Military Police chief Ashot Zakaryan had submitted his resignation. Today, the president dismissed Zakaryan from the post he had held for six years. In another decree, Major General Aram Hovhannisyan was appointed to replace him. From 2023 to 2025, he served as deputy interior minister and police chief.

There are no specific details yet about personnel changes in the Department of Moral and Psychological Support.

In recent days, the Defence Ministry has reported consultations on organising psychological support in the armed forces. To review a report on the psychological assistance provided to the military, the defence minister met professors from Yerevan State University’s Research Centre for Psychology. The ministry is also holding discussions with conscript sergeants and officers serving on duty at military posts.

“The agenda includes issues related to preventing hazing and eliminating inappropriate behaviour in the army,” the ministry said.

Comment

Human rights activist Zhanna Aleksanyan believes:

“The army’s top command, led by Suren Papikyan, must give the public a detailed explanation of the series of deaths.

Has anyone from the army’s top command visited the military unit to establish the circumstances of the soldier’s death and find out what was happening there? I strongly doubt it.

Papikyan did not even visit the military unit in the village of Azat when 15 servicemen died.

On 19 January 2023, a fire broke out in the engineering and sapper company’s premises in the village of Azat, killing 15 servicemen. Three others suffered burns of varying severity.

Then, as now, Nikol Pashinyan spoke on Papikyan’s behalf. He named those responsible and accountable. But he did not explain what the Military Police had to do with the death.

If Pashinyan knows more about the situation in the army and at military units, why is Papikyan still the defence minister?”

Suicides in Armenia’s army: statistics

World.title: White House: China is using Georgia to circumvent US tariffs
World.content:
US tariffs on China

According to a White House report titled The Great Transshipment Scam, China is using third countries, including Georgia, to circumvent US tariffs.

The Trump administration’s report names 40 countries and territories as participants in China’s “shadow shipping network”. The White House says these countries may have helped China circumvent US trade restrictions by transshipping and processing goods destined for the US.

The report divides the economies into three categories:

The first category includes countries and trading blocs that receive significant volumes of China-linked goods but have diversified industrial markets. The White House places Canada, the European Union, India, Israel, Japan, Mexico, South Korea and Taiwan in this group.

The second category includes countries with significant economic integration with China. According to the report, these are Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Turkey and Vietnam.

The third category includes China’s “secondary targets”. The White House considers this group to include relatively small economies such as Georgia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Argentina, Switzerland, Panama, Colombia, Chile, Cambodia and the United Arab Emirates.

According to the report, rerouting Chinese goods through third countries is one of the mechanisms companies use to avoid US tariffs on Chinese imports.

The White House published the report as part of the broader trade policy of the US administration. One of its main goals is to tighten enforcement of restrictions on imports from China and prevent companies from circumventing tariffs through third countries.

In 2025, Georgia imported $1.98 billion worth of goods from China, while its exports to the US amounted to just $120 million.

The value of goods imported from China into Georgia was significantly higher than the value of Georgian exports to the US. According to 2025 data, ferroalloys accounted for the largest category of goods imported from China into Georgia.

During the same period, Georgia’s main exports to the US included power-generating equipment and passenger cars.

Trade data show that Chinese imports account for a significant share of Georgia’s trade with China, while Georgian exports to the US remain relatively small.

US President Donald Trump began imposing and gradually increasing tariffs on Chinese goods in February 2025. By April 2025, the rate had reached 145%. Beijing responded with similar measures, imposing a 125% tariff on US products.

Following talks in May that year, the US cut the newly imposed tariffs from 145% to 30%, while China reduced its tariffs from 125% to 10%. However, other tariffs introduced before 2025 remained in place.

According to data published by the US Congress, various tariffs on Chinese goods are currently in effect under several US laws. Some target China directly, while others apply to specific economic sectors and also affect Chinese goods.

US tariffs on China

World.title: Deportation, ‘international wanted list’ mark new escalation in Baku-Moscow tensions
World.content:
Escalation in Azerbaijani-Russian relations

Two developments on 17 August highlighted the continuing fragility of relations between Baku and Moscow. Russia deported Bakhtiyar Hasanov, chairman of the Azerbaijani National-Cultural Autonomy in Moscow, to Azerbaijan. Azerbaijan, in turn, placed three Russian citizens on an international wanted list: Moscow 24 TV presenter Ivan Knyazev, political consultant and media expert Semyon Uralov, and journalist and adviser to the Russian transport minister Alexei Chadayev.

The fact that the two developments occurred on the same day may at first suggest that they were reciprocal measures. However, the process that culminated in Hasanov’s deportation had begun well before 17 August, with his case under consideration for at least several months. Therefore, while there is no public evidence of a direct causal link between the two decisions, both developments fit into the broader pattern of the prolonged deterioration in Azerbaijani-Russian relations.

Deportation of Bakhtiyar Hasanov

According to open sources, Bakhtiyar Hasanov was detained in Russia in June 2026 and placed in a temporary detention centre for foreign nationals. He appealed against the decision to deport him, but the court rejected his appeal.

According to sources, Hasanov’s Russian citizenship was revoked in September 2025. In autumn 2025, the Agentstvo media outlet established that Hasanov’s passport, issued in 2019, was listed as invalid in a Russian government database. Hasanov himself denied at the time that he had been stripped of his citizenship.

One of the key questions is the legal basis on which his citizenship was revoked. Open sources provide no complete or unequivocal explanation for the decision.

The case also carries political significance because of Hasanov’s status. For many years, he cooperated with official Moscow bodies dealing with diaspora and interethnic relations and served on public councils. His deportation is therefore also being viewed as part of a broader trend of pressure on the Azerbaijani diaspora in Russia.

Growing pressure on the diaspora

Since the summer of 2025, several prominent members of the Azerbaijani diaspora in Russia have been stripped of their citizenship, detained or expelled from the country. The names of Arshad Khankishiyev, Elshan Ibrahimov and Javid Rzayev have been mentioned in this context.

Russian nationalist and Kremlin-aligned media have largely portrayed these measures as part of efforts to combat illegal migration, alleged links to criminal groups and security concerns. However, final court rulings on all the allegations made against these individuals are not publicly available.

This process took on a more overtly political dimension following an operation targeting Azerbaijani families in Yekaterinburg in June 2025. The deaths of the Safarov brothers during the operation prompted a sharp reaction from Baku. Moscow linked the operation to an investigation into crimes committed many years earlier, while the Azerbaijani side focused on reports of violence and torture against those detained.

Since then, the issue of the diaspora has gradually moved beyond the social and cultural sphere and become one of the instruments of political pressure in relations between the two countries.

Baku’s charges against three Russian citizens

On 17 August, Azerbaijan’s Prosecutor General’s Office said that Ivan Knyazev, Semyon Uralov and Alexei Chadayev had been placed on a wanted list as part of a criminal investigation.

The investigation relates to programmes published on Uralov’s YouTube channel on 14 July and 13 August. According to the Azerbaijani authorities, the broadcasts contained calls for the violent overthrow of the country’s constitutional order, violations of its territorial integrity, terrorist activity and incitement of ethnic hatred.

The criminal case is being investigated under Articles 214-2, 281.2 and 283.2.1 of Azerbaijan’s Criminal Code. A court ordered the three men to be detained in absentia.

Excerpts from the broadcasts published by Azerbaijani media include remarks about a possible military operation against Baku, military pressure on Azerbaijan from the Caspian Sea and the use of physical violence against the country’s leadership. However, the Prosecutor General’s Office has not published full transcripts of the broadcasts, expert assessments or all the episodes on which the charges are based.

What do Uralov and Chadayev say?

The accused reject Baku’s allegations. Alexei Chadayev denied inciting ethnic hatred, saying that his criticism was directed not against the Azerbaijani people but against the country’s political leadership.

Semyon Uralov, for his part, described the Azerbaijani authorities’ decision as politically motivated. In subsequent Telegram posts, he continued to sharply criticise the political systems of post-Soviet countries, including the Azerbaijani authorities.

The response indicates that the case has moved beyond the legal sphere and become part of the broader information confrontation between the two countries.

‘International wanted list’ does not mean automatic arrest

The term “international wanted list”, used by Azerbaijani media, does not mean that a wanted person will automatically be arrested in another country.

Even if Interpol issues a Red Notice, it does not constitute an international arrest warrant. Each country decides whether to detain a wanted person in accordance with its own laws. In addition, Interpol’s constitution prohibits the organisation from intervening in matters of a political, military, religious or racial character.

The outcome of Baku’s request will therefore depend on the legal evidence submitted, as well as on how other countries assess the case — as a criminal prosecution or as a continuation of the political confrontation.

Ukraine factor

The latest escalation in Azerbaijani-Russian relations comes against the backdrop of the growing prominence of the Ukraine issue.

On 6 August, Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov made his first official visit to Kyiv since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and visited Irpin. Azerbaijan reiterated its support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders. The two sides also discussed the possibility of supplying Azerbaijani gas to Ukraine.

Against this political backdrop, former Ukrainian President Viktor Yushchenko visited Baku on 16–17 August and met Ilham Aliyev. The presentation to Aliyev of a certificate naming him an honorary citizen of Irpin could be perceived in Moscow as a symbolic political gesture.

There is no evidence confirming a direct link between these developments and Hasanov’s deportation. However, the Azerbaijani leadership’s increasingly open articulation of a position on Ukraine that differs from Moscow’s fits into the broader picture of growing discontent in Russian political circles.

New mechanisms of mutual pressure

One notable change in relations between Baku and Moscow over the past two years has been the increasingly active use of law-enforcement and administrative mechanisms in the context of their political confrontation.

Russia has applied citizenship and migration laws, as well as criminal legislation, against members of the Azerbaijani diaspora. Azerbaijan, in turn, has used criminal prosecution mechanisms against individuals linked to Russian media over statements that Baku regards as posing a threat to the country.

This does not in itself mean that the legal arguments put forward by either side are unfounded. However, the fact that such legal measures are being taken against the backdrop of political crises in bilateral relations inevitably raises questions about their selective application and possible use for political purposes.

Where are relations heading?

At this stage, a complete political rupture between Azerbaijan and Russia appears unlikely. The two countries have significant mutual interests in areas including trade, transport, logistics and regional security.

At the same time, a return to the previous level of relations also appears difficult. Instead, an emerging model seems to be characterised by political mistrust alongside continued, limited cooperation.

Azerbaijanis living in Russia, as well as diaspora organisations maintaining social ties between the two countries, could find themselves particularly vulnerable in this confrontation. The use of diaspora representatives as instruments in an interstate dispute, particularly when accompanied by ethnic rhetoric, increases the risk that tensions could extend beyond diplomatic relations and affect relations between the two societies.

The events of 17 August therefore have broader significance than two separate legal decisions. They point to the emergence of a new model of relations in which Baku and Moscow, while continuing to cooperate, are increasingly making use of political and legal means to exert pressure on one another.

World.title: Previous migration policies 'taking the p*ss' warns migrant rich-lister
World.content:
As political pressure mounts for drastic migration cuts, business leaders warn that could result in critical worker shortages in areas ranging from aged care to construction, urging instead for the public debate to shift away from numbers.

While Labor is yet to land on a final position, the most recent federal budget forecasts have the net overseas migration rate (NOM) falling from about 300,000 to 245,000 people this financial year.

The government's current permanent migration intake is 185,000 places, about 70 per cent of which are skilled workers, with the majority of the remainder their families.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has said she wants to reduce the permanent intake to 130,000.

The Coalition has called for migration to be capped in line with housing construction but not proposed a specific number.

Flight Centre CEO Graham Turner said the tourism sector is only marginally impacted by migration because it relies more heavily on visitors.

Graham Turner says immigration is the main way Australia grows. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

But Mr Turner has long been of the view that population growth, including migration growth, should be sustainable.

"Australia has a limit … and obviously, the world has a limit to how many people we can handle," Mr Turner said.

But he noted "population growth is slowing in a lot of more advanced countries now", and that "immigration, for Australia, is the main way we grow".

"I would say somewhere in that 200,000 to 300,000 a year [range], which is more or less in the middle of the Labor Party's proposals, is probably reasonable," Mr Turner said.

"We're a country of migrants, and they contribute an enormous amount not only to our economy, but to our multicultural society, and most of that, I believe, is quite positive.

"Obviously we can't continue growing forever, but at the moment I think that sort of balance is probably not too bad."

Child migrant rich-lister calls for 'selective' approach

Leading business groups have been arguing against a significant cut to Australia's current net overseas migration intake of roughly 300,000, arguing it could cause skills shortages and damage the economy.

However, ecommerce entrepreneur and rich-lister Ruslan Kogan has pushed back against what he sees as a self-interested view from some elements of the business community.

"I think immigration is a very important area of policy for the building of a nation, and so it needs to be looked at from the nation as a whole perspective, not just what the business community or certain areas of the economy might think is best for them," he told ABC News in an exclusive interview.

Mr Kogan spent the early part of his childhood in communist Belarus before arriving in Melbourne with his parents in 1989, making a mark on the nation's business landscape by setting up several successful ecommerce companies.

After arriving in Australia as a child, Ruslan Kogan built several ecommerce companies, including Kogan.com. (Supplied: kogan.com)

He does not have a specific number in mind for Australia's migrant intake, but argues that because "we have the most amazing country in the world, we can be very selective about the type of immigration we open up to".

"At a company, when we're recruiting people, we would map things out and say, 'Well, what sort of skills are available in the market and who has them and where?'" he said.

"I think you can extrapolate that to a nation to say, 'Well, we want people of certain skill sets and we want to make immigration easier for people that are doctors, engineers, or electricians, or scientists, or whatever skill set it is that we think is the future and that we need more of over here."

Everybody wants to cut migration The causes of migration are murky and it is harder for politicians to control than they would like to admit.

Aside from specific skills and attracting people "who can build things", Mr Kogan also said, "We want people to come here and embrace our culture, embrace our values and the Western way of life."

Asked about the similarity of that view with some of the opinions expressed by One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, Mr Kogan said, "To be honest, I haven't really been watching Pauline Hanson's comments."

"We don't want to change our way of life," Mr Kogan argued.

"We like our Western values. We like our rule of law. We like our very strong and robust legal system and the way that the systems and structures in our society work.

"We think that we've built this amazing, beautiful country. So assimilation is very important.

"The last thing we want is to turn Australia into a shithole."

Aged care, construction warn of staffing crisis if migration slashed

Esha Oberoi is the founder and co-CEO of Leora Healthcare, which provides aged care and disability services nationally.

Esha Oberoi says the aged care industry is reliant on migrants. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

She migrated to Australia from India when she was seven years old, and was an aged care worker herself, before founding her business in 2008.

She warned a cut to the migration intake would be damaging because her business would not be able to source the skilled workers it needs to care for older and disabled Australians.

"We employ close to 800 employees and over 45 per cent of them are on [working or student] visas," Ms Oberoi told ABC News.

She estimated one in six aged care workers are on a visa industry-wide.

"There is a huge dependency for us on immigration. We know that in the next decade, nearly 1.5 million people over the age of 65 are going to enter the aged care system," she said.

"That requires 400,000 aged care workers and I just, I don't know how we are going to be able to provide Australians the level of care that they deserve as they're aging.

"If we consider cutting down on immigration as a blanket rule, I just don't how this is going to work."

She said work in the sector "is one of the most emotionally challenging, one of most physically taxing", and that there are not enough Australians willing to do it.

"We're talking about people doing five different shifts in a day, going from job to job for two hours on a minimum wage — it's really not the most glamorous job that you can find," she said.

" We don't have people just lining up for this work, but what we do know is that our Indian immigrants, our Nepalese, the Chinese, the Vietnamese, these people, they come and enrich one, this nation, but they're actually doing this hard work. "

The residential construction industry is another that relies heavily on its migrant workforce.

Brad Duggan is the chief executive of Metricon, Australia's largest residential home builder.

Brad Duggan has observed migrant communities becoming skilled in particular trades. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

While Metricon has seen a 40 per cent fall in inquiries to build new homes, and a drop in the migration intake could further dent demand, Mr Duggan said the bigger issue is the reliance on skilled workers to do building work Australians do not want to do.

"There's been this overemphasis on the importance of getting a tertiary education, and that we've really focused our kids to think that's the only way to build wealth and be successful," he said.

"You will find most of our plastering crews are normally from an Asian background. Some of the best, if not the best, rendering crews are from Afghani backgrounds.

"Large communities have come in and taken up responsibility for certain trades and they're a really important part of the Australian residential housing industry."

Metricon has lobbied government ministers to not cut migration. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Mr Duggan has been meeting with Australia's housing minister on the issue and has urged federal politicians to steer clear of emotive debates and look at the facts.

"Let's not focus on what is the popular solution," Mr Duggan said.

"I've lived all over the world, Australia is a great place to live and I know why migration is quite high, but I don't see migration of people coming in with skilled trades taking jobs away from Australians.

"We need more and more of them [migrants] so we can build more homes, so I don't think that should be something that we're fearful of as a country."

'We came here to be Australians and contribute'

Mr Kogan said when he and his family arrived in Australia it was common to see migrants "coming here and starting businesses, working really hard, learning English, integrating into our society, wanting to become Aussies".

Ruslan Kogan's parents migrated to Australia with their two children and $90 in their pockets. (Supplied: Ruslan Kogan)

"That is exactly what my family did in 1989 when they came to Australia with $90 in their pocket," he said.

"You know, my parents arrived here and wanted to learn what it's like to throw a few shrimps on the barbie."

Mr Kogan does not fret about the number of migrants arriving but said he is more worried about the type of migrants that are allowed to come.

"The wrong kind of migrant, I think, would be somebody looking to Australia from a 'what's in it for me perspective?'" Mr Kogan said.

Mr Turner said, "Obviously every country's got to regulate their immigration": "No system will ever be perfect on this."

"I think the wrong type of migrant is probably someone who doesn't particularly want to work, who's looking to come because of the social welfare benefits or something like that," he said.

"But I would suspect that from what I've seen, and I don't know the stats on this, that's a pretty small minority of people who are coming to this country."

Graham Turner says Australia needs people who want to work and contribute. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

He said to attract migrants who want to contribute economically, "education is very important".

" I think it is a fair bit about getting the right people in here preferably. Certainly other than refugees, making sure that the people we get as permanent migrants can contribute to our society. "

Loading...

'People think politicians have been taking the p*ss'

Regardless of what the final migrant intake number is, Mr Kogan thinks the federal government should "be very selective" about which type of migrant they let in, although he is uncertain exactly how they would police it.

ABC Business Daily The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news.

While he has faced his own controversy in recent years — in 2020 the Federal Court found that his company Kogan Australia breached Australian consumer law during a tax-time promotion — he said he and his family have always tried to give back to the country that gave them opportunities to flourish.

"If you start bringing in amazing migrants with great skills who are contributing to society, who are assimilating and become taxpayers … then I'm sure there will be very few people complaining about cutting numbers or raising numbers, or any of those minor details," he said.

"There's a great Aussie saying that I very often use, and it's, 'don't piss on me back and tell me it's raining'. And I think that the Australian public and voter base are very smart and I think they know how to call bullshit when they see it.

"I would suspect that … people think that the politicians have been taking the piss with the current policies and doing things that are not in the best interest of the public and the population."

Watch The Business, Mondays to Thursdays 8:44pm on ABC News Channel, after the Late News on ABC TV, and anytime on ABC iview.

World.title: Fish feed giant Skretting fires back over Facebook claims of contamination
World.content:
Biosecurity Tasmania has confirmed it is investigating a fish food contamination claim at a major manufacturer after an employee resigned and posted a series of images online.

On Friday morning, Matthew Levien, 36, resigned from his position as team leader at Skretting Australia's facility at Cambridge, Hobart, after alerting the production manager about mouldy feed being processed back into pellets.

Matthew Levien says he complained to his supervisors, to no avail. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Mr Levien, who quit his job at Skretting after less than two weeks, is a trained aquaculture technician and captain who has worked in the industry for about 15 years, including at barramundi farms, oyster farms and pearl farms.

He also has qualifications in compliance, health and safety and food hygiene.

Fish feed pellets, as they appear on the Skrettings website. (Skrettings)

A photo by Mark Levien of fish feed at the Skretting factory. (Supplied: Matthew Levien)

In his second week, during which he was put on a regular roster, Mr Levien said he was in the facility's intake area where he saw mouldy fish feed pellets "getting reworked back into new pellets".

"I raised that with the operators who worked there and they said, 'Oh, it's common' [and] 'it's a bag every now and then' and they were under the assumption the rework process burns off the mycotoxins," he said.

" The rework process doesn't burn off the mycotoxins. "

New South Wales's SafeWork agency defines mycotoxins as "naturally occurring toxins produced by certain moulds", which are "dangerous to humans and can cause serious health problems".

Skretting is the world's largest producer of feeds for industrially farmed fish. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Mr Levien said he "raised it with managers and they told me the same thing".

He said he noted "pigeons roosting as well and laying eggs in the intake area where the raw product goes in for rework".

"I did mention this to one of the senior team leaders and he said he's been trying to get them to clean it for years and that it's a very ongoing problem," he said.

" If anyone has a basic understanding of biohazardous material, birds are a real big one. The feathers, the fecal matter and the eggs from those birds present a whole lot of health risks. "

Skrettings supplies fish feed to the Tasmanian salmon industry. (Supplied: Bob Brown Foundation)

Mr Levien took photos and video to provide evidence of his concerns.

After his concerns were minimised by his supervisor, he decided to resign and lodged a formal complaint with Biosecurity Tasmania.

In his written complaint, which has been seen by the ABC, Mr Levien wrote that the severity of the breach he had witnessed at Skretting "cannot be overstated" and posed a grave risk.

"Fish Health: The presence of mold indicates potential mycotoxin contamination, which can cause severe health complications, reduced growth, immune suppression, and mass mortality in fish populations. "Human Health: Contaminated feed presents a risk of mycotoxins entering the human food chain through fish consumption, posing long-term food safety risks."

"Despite these clear dangers, management was fully aware of this practice and chose to ignore it," Mr Levien wrote.

Compounding these concerns, Mr Levien said the facility suffered from severe structural and vector contamination issues:

"Pigeon Contamination: Pigeon faecal matter is visibly present directly in the intake area for raw products, creating a direct vector for biological pathogens. "Feral Pests: Feral cats are present throughout the warehouse environment, further compromising sanitation and contamination controls."

Matthew Levien fired back at claims that he is merely a disgruntled employee. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Mr Levien said he was told by an officer at Biosecurity Tasmania that his complaint would be investigated but that it might take days before the agency was able to inspect Skretting's Cambridge facility.

The regulator's reaction prompted Mr Levien to share his photos on Facebook.

"I felt it was my duty to inform the public," he said.

"I didn't have confidence they would go to the facility. I was told directly that we can't go there right now. And I know that companies as large as this one have enough financial backing to completely sweep these sorts of practices under a rug."

A Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania spokesperson told the ABC that Biosecurity Tasmania was aware of the allegations and is investigating the matter but would not comment further.

Independent Member for Franklin Peter George, who was contacted by Mr Levien on the weekend, wrote to Primary Industries Minister Gavin Pearce on Saturday describing the allegations as "credible and serious" and calling for a "full, urgent and transparent investigation".

Skretting describes itself as "a world leader in the manufacture and supply of aquaculture feeds, making us an essential link in the feed-to-food chain". (Tassal)

'No food safety risk', Skretting says

Skretting Australia issued a statement on Saturday that it was "aware of social media posts and allegations made by a former employee".

"We recognise that the images in the post are concerning when viewed without the correct context and facts," it said.

"In this case, the product identified in the post had developed mould during storage and was contained during the intake process, before any related post appeared on social media. The product remains isolated, awaiting disposal, and it was not, and will not be, incorporated into feed production.

" There is no food safety risk and no fish will consume this feed. "

Skretting, which is a major supplier to the aquaculture industry in Tasmania and nationally, is a global business with billions of dollars in turnover, employing more than 3,000 people in 18 countries.

Headquartered in Norway, it is a division of Nutreco, in turn owned by private Dutch trading company SHV Holdings.

In a statement to the ABC yesterday, Skretting said that it took Mr Levien's allegations "seriously, but we do not accept the suggestion that mould-contaminated material is purposefully being reworked into feed production at our Cambridge facility".

Skretting said that finished feed was routinely tested by an independent third-party laboratory for undesirable substances, including mycotoxins and aflatoxins.

All testing undertaken in 2026 and 2025 returned results below detection thresholds, it said.

"We are aware concerns have been referred to Biosecurity Tasmania and will cooperate fully with any enquiries from the relevant regulatory authorities," Skretting's statement said.

" We will not speculate on the motivations of a former employee or comment publicly on individual employment matters. "

Main risk to salmon, expert says

Christian Narkowicz, a senior lecturer in pharmacology at the University of Tasmania, told the ABC that it was very common for fungi to infect salmon feed.

"Especially as they've gone to a lot of plant-based ingredients in salmon feed. It's a more common occurrence now than when it was mostly fish-based feed," Dr Narkowicz said.

"I'm not surprised to see so much mould growing in salmon feed, especially if it hasn't been stored appropriately."

How many salmon farms are there in Tasmania — and who owns them? Those black, circular things floating in the water off the Tasmanian coastline? They are salmon farms. Here is how many there are — and who owns them.

Dr Narkowicz said the main risk, if there was one, would be to the health of the salmon.

"It's been shown that mycotoxins in salmon feed impact their health, can damage their liver and also reduce their immunity, which makes them more susceptible to other kinds of diseases.

"It's also been shown that mycotoxins that are consumed by salmon do enter the flesh of the salmon. Now, whether that's a human health issue or not, I think is yet to be determined.

" I think it's fair to say that mycotoxins are hazardous to humans and can affect the health of humans, which is why there are regulatory limits on the concentration of mycotoxins that are permitted in food. "

Dr Narkowicz said whether or not the levels in Skretting's fish feed exceeded the regulatory limits was "yet to be determined".

'Not something I would expose lightly'

Mr Levien's Facebook posts have sparked debate, with a number of people claiming to have worked at Skretting also suggesting poor practices were common.

Other posters suggested Mr Levien was a disgruntled ex-employee, which he rejects, saying the position at Skretting was "a dream job for me".

"What employee starts at a company for two weeks, quits a $130,000 job, puts his name on the line across social media?" he said.

"What person does that for their own benefit? I probably won't be hired in this industry again across the whole of Australia.

"I love this industry. I love the marine industry. I've farmed for 15 years. So it's not something that I would expose lightly.

"Even if I was disgruntled, I wouldn't release such a bombshell for myself.

"It's something I'm concerned about. I think people eating this food need to know what goes into it. The facility should have extra cleaners and extra operators on the floor.

World.title: The IDF investigated itself and found possible 'criminal misconduct' in Gaza
World.content:
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) has published the findings of five internal probes that examined deadly attacks its soldiers launched on aid and medical workers in Gaza.

The information released on Wednesday represents the IDF's largest single information dump relating to civilian deaths since the war erupted in October 2023.

Two of the most high-profile cases are now the subject of criminal investigations by military police, Israel's military revealed on Wednesday.

However, in the other three cases, including one in which Australian charity worker Zomi Frankcom was killed, soldiers have been cleared of wrongdoing.

Loading

The findings were published by the General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism (FFAM).

The FFAM is part of Israel's military and is responsible for launching initial investigations into suspected war crimes and judging whether they should be expanded.

The way Israel's military investigates itself has been criticised by human rights groups in and outside the country for not taking allegations of war crimes seriously enough.

"A system that overwhelmingly closes cases without accountability, years after the fact, and only in response to sustained international pressure, is not justice, it's a whitewash," a spokesperson for prominent NGO Human Rights Watch told the ABC after the IDF published its findings.

Here's what you need to know about the information released on Wednesday.

Criminal investigation opened into killing of Hind Rajab

For the first time, the IDF has acknowledged it opened fire on the vehicle carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab and her family members.

One of the mostly widely condemned incidents of the war, Rajab initially survived an attack on her family's vehicle as they fled Gaza City on January 29, 2025.

Surrounded by her relatives' corpses, she answered a call from the Palestinian Red Crescent Society and stayed on the line for hours in the bullet-ridden car.

The line was cut amid the sound of gunfire. A recording of Rajab's hours-long plea was broadcast globally, drawing international condemnation.

Hind Rajab's body was recovered 12 days after the car her family was in was shot up by the IDF. (AFP: Family Handout)

In February 2025, the IDF said its initial investigation suggested no troops were in the area at the time of the incident.

However on Wednesday, it conceded for the first time soldiers had fired on the car Rajab was in, and the ambulance that had attempted to rescue her had also had "a shell fired towards it".

Rajab's body was found 12 days later alongside six family members and two paramedics.

On Wednesday the IDF said this incident was now the subject of a criminal probe being handled by the Military Police Criminal Investigation Division (MPCID), the Israeli military's main arm for investigating allegations of criminal offences.

Rajab's story inspired an Oscar-nominated film called The Voice of Hind Rajab and the formation of legal non-profit organisation The Hind Rajab Foundation, which said it had "no confidence in the Israeli military's reported decision to open criminal investigations".

Criminal investigation opened after IDF soldiers killed Palestinian paramedics

The IDF also announced on Wednesday a criminal investigation had been opened after Israeli soldiers killed 15 Palestinians, including Red Crescent paramedics, in southern Gaza on March 23, 2025.

This incident attracted significant international attention at the time. The IDF on Wednesday said its MPCID had initiated a probe because "the firing conducted during the incident raises a reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct".

The IDF claims in the early hours of the morning of March 23, its soldiers opened fire on several rescue vehicles in the Tel al-Sultan refugee camp, near Rafah, in three separate incidents over the course of about 90 minutes.

"It later became apparent that the vehicles struck in the first and second shooting incidents were a fire truck and ambulances, and that the vehicle struck in the third shooting incident was a Palestinian UN vehicle," the IDF statement released this week read.

The IDF claimed that across the three incidents it killed a total of 15 Palestinians, six of which it said were Hamas militants.

But it conceded "medical personnel and paramedics" were also among the victims. It said a commander had already been reprimanded, and a deputy commander had been fired over the incident.

In a statement, the Palestinian Red Crescent Society said it wanted the formation of an "independent international commission of inquiry to uncover the circumstances of this crime".

IDF will not continue investigating strike that killed Australian woman

The IDF announced on Wednesday there would be no criminal investigation into a strike on April 1, 2024 that killed seven humanitarian workers, including Australian woman Zomi Frankcom, travelling in a charity organisation's convoy.

The IDF said it had concluded there were serious failures that led soldiers to falsely identify a Hamas fighter was travelling in the convoy, which actually belonged to the food charity World Central Kitchen (WCK)

While Israel's military claimed there was an armed man travelling with the vehicles, it said it now understood that person was a security guard.

In the findings released on Wednesday, the IDF claimed it "mistakenly believed that the vehicles contained Hamas military operatives and therefore struck the vehicles".

Zomi Frankcom had worked for WCK for several years before she was killed in an IDF strike. (Supplied: Facebook)

Despite the fact there will be no criminal investigation, two IDF commanders have already been stripped of their ranks as colonel and major, and a colonel, a major general and a brigadier general have also been reprimanded over the incident.

In a statement, WCK described the IDF's decision as "deeply offensive".

"The military investigation conflates different timelines and events, muddies the story and shifts the blame for the IDF's illegal conduct," it read.

"We continue to demand truth and justice for our team and their families."

No criminal probe into IDF killing of Médecins Sans Frontières employees

The last two attacks addressed in Wednesday's IDF statement involved the killing of Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) employees in the enclave's south.

The first took place early on February 20, 2024 when the IDF struck a building in the southern area of Khan Yunis which they said was "later found to belong to Médecins Sans Frontières".

Two women were killed in the attack, and seven others were injured. Wednesday's statement claimed IDF troops identified a building overlooking a route they "did not operationally control … near Hamas combat compounds where the presence of enemy forces in the area and its surroundings was expected".

The statement claimed the building was situated in a location that posed a threat, adding that the lights were off and there was no movement.

Under international law, objects may be attacked in certain circumstances if they qualify as a military target by their "nature, location, purpose or use" or if they make an "effective contribution to military action".

In cases of doubt, a typically civilian object should be presumed not to be used for military purposes.

According to an MSF statement at the time of the attack, an Israeli tank fired on a house where MSF employees and their families were staying.

The IDF review concluded the troops fired for a military purpose at what they assessed to be a military objective, and that there was no basis to initiate a criminal probe.

However, the statement did say that "certain faults" had been identified during the attack, which would be dealt directly with relevant commanders.

A boy inspects the site of an Israeli strike on the shelter belonging to MSF in Khan Younis. (Reuters: Mohammed Salem)

The second attack involving MSF employees discussed in Wednesday's statement took place on November 18, 2023 in Gaza City.

The IDF statement claimed a miscommunication between military authorities and soldiers at a checkpoint meant an MSF convoy that had approval to travel between the charity's facilities in the north and south of the strip was stopped and told to wait.

The IDF claimed the convoy ignored instructions to wait and attempted to return to Gaza City without permission and that Israeli soldiers fired "warning shots" towards the road.

In its findings, the IDF claimed there was a "possibility" two passengers in the convoy were killed "by bullet ricochet or bullet splash from the warning fire".

The ABC has contacted MSF for comment.

World.title: Qld government asked to withdraw youth justice bill over concerns for Indigenous children
World.content:
Australia's commissioner for First Nations children has penned a scathing letter to the Queensland government, urging it to scrap proposed controversial legislation to deliver youth offender bootcamps.

In her letter, the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People Commissioner Sue-Anne Hunter asked for the Youth Justice (Circuit Breaker) Amendment Bill to be withdrawn.

She said those who voted for the bill to be passed would be supporting a model which could hide the abuse of children and would unfairly target First Nations youth.

"So the question I ask each of you to answer, on the record, is this: will you vote for a model under which harm to a child, the State has placed hundreds of kilometres away from their home, need not be reported by the adults responsible, cannot be escalated by the child, and cannot be found by an independent inspector?" Commissioner Hunter said.

Youth boot camp concerns The Queensland government wants to allow Circuit Breaker Program operators to not report child harm if doing so would incriminate themselves. Welfare groups say this could harm children.

Child welfare agencies have previously condemned the proposed camps, as camp operators would have a "reasonable" excuse not to report any harm to a child, if doing so could incriminate them.

The laws would introduce a court-ordered alternative to detention, and mean children could be sent to one of two remote properties with a service provider for up to six months.

Participants would be required to wear an electronic monitoring device and would be given basic education and hands-on learning in agriculture and livestock management.

The circuit breaker legislation has drawn parallels to the former Newman government's controversial boot camps, which were trialled in 2013.

A blowout in the cost of running the camps, as well as a string of mishaps, led to their being shut down in 2015 by then-attorney-general Yvette D'ath.

An evaluation of the boot camps found they had failed to cut repeat offending, with more than half of the young people sentenced going on to reoffend.

Minister for Youth Justice Laura Gerber introduced the bill in June. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

Bill needs to be 'rebuilt'

The Justice, Integrity and Community Safety Committee last week recommended the laws be passed without amendment.

Commissioner Hunter, in her letter, pointed out that another section of the proposed legislation would allow a child's complaints to be silenced if they are considered trivial or would cause annoyance.

"A child held at these places also has no statutory right to escalate a concern to the Queensland Ombudsman, the Queensland Family and Child Commission or the Public Guardian," she said.

"Adults have a lawful reason not to report harm, and children have no reliable way to raise it themselves. That is the design the Queensland Parliament is being asked to approve."

The Crisafulli government ran on a tough on youth crime agenda. (ABC News: Cameron Simmons)

Commissioner Hunter also said, in her letter, the bill needed to be "rebuilt" with First Nations people "at the table".

"The reality is that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children will bear the weight of this program," she said in the letter.

"These are not big asks. They are just seeking what is fair and in line with human rights.

"Children cannot vote. You can. Think about the consequences."

Youth Justice Minister Laura Gerber has been contacted for comment.

When introducing the bill to parliament in June, Ms Gerber said it was designed to be a "genuine alternative to sentencing a youth to detention".

"It is about rehabilitation that actually works," she told the House. "It is about making sure there are fewer victims of crime in this state. "

World.title: Labor has made the most of its cooperation with the Coalition
World.content:
In the last term of parliament, Anthony Albanese would often delight in calling Peter Dutton "Captain No", for being "against everything and for nothing".

It was a regular, if not entirely original, line of Labor attack. Before "Captain No" there was "Dr No", Tony Abbott.

But it will be hard for Labor to pin a similar badge on Angus Taylor after the bipartisanship on display this week.

The opposition leader has said "yes", multiple times, after a series of meetings with the prime minister last week.

The opposition leader has said "yes", multiple times, after a series of meetings with the prime minister last week. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

A display of cooperation

From gambling ads to the NDIS, forcing social media giants to pay for journalism and avoiding a so-called "Widow's Tax", the two sides of politics have demonstrated a rare degree of cooperation.

"We're not the party who says no to everything," noted the Liberals' Andrew Hastie on Radio National, in a nod to the old Dutton moniker. "We want to work constructively in the national interest."

Hastie is on the frontline of the Liberal Party's fight with One Nation and it is impossible to ignore this backdrop.

This week has been an opportunity for the Coalition to differentiate itself from Pauline Hanson. It is demonstrating its credentials as a sensible party of government, rather than a party of protest.

There were other motivations too, on both sides, for all this deal-making.

For the Coalition, gambling advertising had become a point of internal division between anti-regulation libertarians on one side and those who wanted much tighter restrictions on the other, including three who ultimately crossed the floor to vote against the bill.

"This an emotional issue," observed Taylor, who was "very pleased" to see the long-running debate put to bed.

Labor faced its own internal pushback too, even if none were willing to risk being expelled from the party for crossing the floor under party rules.

The bipartisan deal involves a new, complex set of rules on gambling advertising, and many operational and technical details still to be worked out.

Advocates who wanted a complete ban have been left bitterly disappointed, but both leaders are betting the pressure will ease with a bill now passed.

Loading...

Taylor protects fiscal credibility

On the NDIS, the disability sector is equally disappointed with the outcome, but the Coalition's eventual support for Labor's changes was never in serious doubt.

With the cost of the scheme still growing at more than 10 per cent annually, Taylor's fiscal credibility would have been shot if he'd delayed much longer.

Political risks for Labor still lie ahead as these changes are put in place, stories emerge of people with a disability being removed from the NDIS or having their supports cut.

NDIS Minister Mark Butler concedes there's still a "tonne of work" to do in setting up alternative supports.

States and territories are hardly sounding confident these supports will be there on time. The concerns being expressed by families is understandable.

NDIS changes get through Senate The controversial changes to the NDIS have passed the Senate after Labor struck a deal with the Coalition, tabling 63 amendments to the reforms.

Given the political sensitivities and potential landmines, this bipartisan deal on the NDIS was arguably the most significant of the week.

It gives the government some political cover for what lies ahead, underpins any hope of budget repair, and is aimed at maintaining community support for this transformative scheme.

For the prime minister, the aim was to do all these deals with the Coalition in one go. He wanted to ensure the decks were clear for this to be "Liberal deal week".

Albanese didn't want other issues, including the government's soon-to-be-announced immigration changes, causing distractions and demands for more cross-trading.

In the end, the biggest concession required from Labor to seal the deal wasn't much of a concession at all. It agreed to expedite something it had already agreed to do: passing a bill to avoid a "Widow's Tax" when someone loses a partner who was negatively gearing a property.

Labor has two pathways through the Senate. It framed the May budget with this in mind.

The Greens have already helped pass negative gearing and capital gains tax hikes. They will be called on again when it comes to legislating changes to trusts.

This was the week to get business done with the Coalition.

Nearing the midway point of this parliamentary term, the prospects of cooperation will only diminish as the next election draws closer.

Fights over immigration, superannuation, housing, tobacco excise, data centre rules, and all sorts of other issues will continue and intensify.

But this was a week for cooperation.

Loading

David Speers is national political lead and host of Insiders, which airs on ABC TV at 9am on Sunday or on iview.

World.title: Scam payments lead to an Australian business and its Israeli owner
World.content:
Hooked up to a drip and awaiting surgery, Rodger was running out of options.

"You guys have all of my money tied up," he texted his broker. "I need … to buy a wheelchair."

Having put about $125,000 into an investment platform called The FBTC, he'd run into problems withdrawing his money.

He'd followed instructions from someone claiming to be a financial professional in Switzerland, who was now failing to return any of his money.

Rodger needed to switch to a new bank, the broker said. His account was frozen. There were liquidity issues. He had to pay a fee. The excuses went on and on.

In the meantime, Rodger had to scrounge around to pay his medical bills.

He became increasingly desperate, telling his tormentor that he couldn't even afford to buy Christmas presents for his family that year.

"Sorry to hear that Rodger," came the reply. "If you manage to come up with the 5k [more to invest] … would be perfect."

He never heard from his broker again. His money was gone.

The Sapphire Network

Rodger had fallen victim to an investment fraud group headquartered in Israel.

It is a decentralised network made up of dozens of companies and hundreds of people that has been operating since at least 2021.

More than 4,000 Australians have been targeted to date, often through fake news articles and false promises of AI-assisted trading. Once victims put their money in, they rarely see it again.

The scam group — dubbed the Sapphire Network — is known to operate out of central Tel Aviv and has been linked to call centres in Bulgaria, Ukraine, Cyprus, Macedonia and Israel.

Investigators at the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) estimate that the Sapphire Network has defrauded its victims of hundreds of millions of dollars, entirely through investment scams.

A call centre run by an Israeli company with links to the Sapphire Network. (Facebook: Sara Ieo)

Now, an ABC investigation has identified a network of companies that received payments from its victims, using documents from inside the Sapphire Network, which were leaked to Swedish broadcaster, SVT, and shared with the OCCRP in 2025.

Two reporting partners of the OCCRP — Swedish media foundation Qurium and the amaBhungane Centre for Investigative Journalism — also contributed to this investigation.

Fake articles, made-up names and invented debts

Rodger was scammed by operatives working with the Sapphire Network in June 2024.

Two years later another Australian man, who we'll call Toby, was caught in the same trap. He was lured in by a fake news article, published on an almost-perfect clone of the ABC website.

Perfect dupes of ABC articles are fuelling an industrial-scale scam A global scam is targeting Australians using AI-generated images of ABC journalists and politicians.

Over several months in early 2026, Toby was convinced to part with more than $500,000.

Toby deposited the money into a bank account that his broker told him was set up in his own name, but that he was not in control of. He was then able to trade in the oil and gold markets on the broker's platform.

As the Strait of Hormuz closed and opened again, Toby and his broker discussed the effects on global markets, sharing links to news articles about the US-Iran conflict.

As the trades played out, Toby saw his money multiplying on the dashboard.

But the entire situation was fake. There were no trades and Toby's money was already long gone.

Just like Rodger had been two years earlier, Toby was eventually subjected to psychological tricks and pressure tactics. After some trades supposedly went wrong, he was told that he was in debt for hundreds of thousands of dollars.

A screenshot of the trading platform that Toby was signed up to.

To pay down the fake debt, the scammers suggested that he apply for a range of loans against his home and business.

As they ran through their well-worn playbook, Toby and Rodger's "brokers" hid their identities and tried to avoid accountability.

They operated under fake names and communicated through encrypted messaging apps. They sent their victims fake documents in the name of non-existent companies.

But all the money they stole was real and it left behind a paper trail.

Do you know more? Contact Julian Fell at tips@jtfell.com if you have any information about investment scams.

The receipt that led to a money laundering front

In the early stages of the scam, Toby's broker had asked for a small payment to open an account on the fraudulent trading platform.

This is a common tactic to onboard potential victims, ensuring they have money on the line early.
