These initial payments — usually for about $350 — are often disguised as payments for online courses or immigration services. But this is only an accounting trick to pass them off as legitimate transactions.

In Toby's case, the payment went to a company called Trigo XO, which was based in the Melbourne suburb of Toorak.

The receipt for Toby’s scam payment to Trigo XO. (Supplied)

The rest of Toby's money was sent to a bank account, which the ABC has been unable to trace to an owner.

But the more modest payment made to Trigo XO proved more fruitful.

Trigo XO operates three websites, each of which advertise online courses. When we tried to purchase courses on these sites, the cracks in this cover story immediately started to show.

No-one answered the phone number listed on the sites and the online checkouts were broken, displaying error after error when we tried to purchase a course.

After sending $365 to Trigo XO, another Australian scam victim was emailed a course in business leadership by Trigo XO.

It consisted of a 35-page PDF document, filled with generic platitudes about leadership.

The business leadership course that no-one asked for. (Trigo XO educational materials)

When we contacted Trigo XO's accountant about Toby's payment and the malfunctioning course sites, he expressed concern about the operation of the business.

The accountant said he'd already made a complaint to Australia's anti-money laundering regulator AUSTRAC, as he had "no way to check" that the invoices coming through Trigo XO were legitimate. (An AUSTRAC spokesperson said the regulator could not comment on or confirm investigations into individual businesses.)

The accountancy firm, director and sole shareholder all cut ties with the company after being contacted by the ABC.

The ABC does not suggest that Trigo XO or anyone associated with it was actively defrauding prospective investors through fake news articles or deceptive phone calls.

Rather, the company appeared to be used to launder payments made as part of the scam's operation.

Its role was to disguise the payments as sales of online courses for its ultimate owner.

The true owner of Trigo XO

Trigo XO's director said the real owner of the company was based in Israel. He then set up a call with someone named Shefi Goldberg.

On the phone, Goldberg insisted that all questions about the business should come to him rather than to his Australian colleagues. "We didn't have any fraudulent activity," he said.

Goldberg's name was not on the company's official filings with Australia's business registry and he provided no proof that he owned Trigo XO.

Goldberg later tried to distance himself from the company, telling Swedish media foundation Qurium he had no link at all.

"I have no ownership, control, or any corporate involvement of any kind with Trigo XO Pty Ltd," Goldberg said in a statement seen by the ABC.

However, a close look at Goldberg's wider business interests leads right back to the Sapphire Network and financial scams.

Shefi Goldberg at a call centre in Israel in 2018. (Facebook: Sara Ieo)

Goldberg is co-director of GoBe Marketing, which has operated call centres in Israel, Cyprus, South Africa, Spain and the Philippines. Its main business is selling visa services via telemarketing, mostly for immigration to the US and Canada.

A South African offshoot of GoBe Marketing, called MSG Marketing, was found to be processing payments for an investment scam in 2021, according to a South African court judgement.

MSG Marketing, which had no financial licence in the country, had misrepresented these transactions as immigration related. The payments were then flagged as suspicious or fraudulent by its bank.

"I was never involved in processing any of such payments," Goldberg said.

And then there's a third company, also linked to Goldberg, which received payments from Australian victims of the Sapphire Network back in 2024.

Victims logged in scammers' spreadsheet

Payments from two Australian scam victims were made to USC Market Place, an Israeli company that lists an employee of GoBe Marketing as its director.

New South Wales Mid North Coast resident Susan paid $378.50 to Finterex Capital, an unregulated trading platform that was later added to Australia's MoneySmart watchlist.

The ABC found Susan's contact details — and this exact payment – logged in the Sapphire Network's internal spreadsheets, along with those of another 4,000 Australian victims.

Susan was later refunded when she disputed the charge.

Two payments from another Australian victim named Anna also line up exactly with the scammers' internal spreadsheet. The fraudulent platform she interacted with, Ambit Capital, was named alongside her transactions.

When asked about Susan's payment, Goldberg texted back: "Sorry but I have no clue about any of this".

And yet, the Sapphire Network's internal documents contained another clue about his involvement.

Goldberg's fingerprints in the Sapphire Network

In a screen recording leaked from inside the Sapphire Network, a back-office worker is surveilled as they toil away in a spreadsheet.

The video shows an inside view of the scam network's money laundering operation, in which a payment processor called Smart Pay plays a starring role.

On one monitor, the worker pulls information from the Smart Pay dashboard.

A screenshot of a Sapphire Network staffer using the Smart Pay dashboard to log payments. (Supplied: OCCRP)

On their other screen they log payments in a similar spreadsheet to the ones where we found Anna's and Susan's payment details.

Later, the worker switches to an encrypted message thread titled "Smart pay — ScholarCloset", and continues their mind-numbing work of logging payments.

Several other videos in the leak connect this payment processor to Shefi Goldberg.

Smart Pay was integrated into the Sapphire Network’s payment processing infrastructure. (Supplied: OCCRP)

A spreadsheet of transactions is shared by an email address info@smart-pay.biz — the main email address of a company called Allegiant Holdings Ltd. That company previously traded as Smart Pay.

The same company name appears in another video, in which someone named Ronen demonstrates how to create payment invoices for $US250 each — the exact cost of the initial charge made to many scam victims.

Company records show that this company, Allegiant Holdings Ltd, is registered in Cyprus and is not to be confused with the unrelated Allegiant Holdings Ltd registered in the UK.

When first asked about Allegiant Holdings Ltd, Goldberg denied owning any entities in Cyprus. But the company registration documents tell a different story: Shefi Goldberg is the sole shareholder.

It's another link between Goldberg and the Sapphire Network, in addition to the scam payments made to three separate companies connected to his business.

Goldberg later said in a statement, "with respect to the Cypriot company, it is used for the provision of services. I am merely registered in connection with the company and am not involved in the management or day-to-day operation of its business."

It has been two years since Rodger was scammed by the Sapphire Network. He's moved on with his life, having given up on getting his money back.

But for Toby, the effects are still fresh. He is trying to make sense of the tricks that were played on him, the lies he was told and the half a million dollars he is unlikely to ever get back.

How we reported this story

World.title: Public servants repay hundreds of thousands of dollars in personal charges
World.content:
Public servants have had to hand back hundreds of thousands of dollars in inadvertent personal charges, including food delivery orders, incurred on taxpayer-funded credit cards.

New figures provided to the Senate detail thousands of transactions in the past financial year where workers across multiple departments breached credit card rules.

At the Home Affairs Department, employees were required to repay 477 purchases made between July last year and March this year worth $28,400.

The accidental personal purchases included 149 transactions valued at about $5,500 that were related to Uber or Uber Eats.

A spokesperson for the department said all private expenditure must be repaid and it had processes to "support the appropriate use" of credit cards.

Katy Gallagher is confident the "system is working". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"Accidental personal expenditure can arise across a range of categories, for example purchases from restaurants, fast food and convenience stores as well as taxis," they said.

Public servants at the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) were also required to repay roughly $151,000 in personal charges last financial year.

The biggest of the 2,029 inadvertent transactions was worth more than $3,000, which was repaid in full.

A DFAT spokesperson noted its policies banned private expenditure on corporate credit cards and said any personal transaction charged in error must be repaid.

At the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, workers had to reimburse 81 inadvertent purchases worth about $2,400, with most of them relating to Uber.

In a statement, Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said she had confidence in the processes in place to manage credit card usage in departments and agencies.

Pollies charge taxpayers $1.1m for family travel in 12 months Family reunion travel is under scrutiny as new analysis shows federal MPs and senators spent $1.1 million on flying and driving their loved ones to Canberra and around Australia in 12 months.

"The information presented shows that the system is working — in that inappropriate use is identified and paid back," she said.

"Agencies and secretaries are required to manage this appropriately at departmental level."

However, Deputy Opposition Leader Jane Hume said thousands of inappropriate transactions across government raised legitimate questions about whether existing controls were sufficiently effective.

"While it is encouraging that these purchases are identified and the vast majority repaid, the scale is concerning," she said.

AFP among agencies and departments misusing credit cards

The Australian Federal Police (AFP) also recorded 987 erroneous personal transactions on corporate credit cards last financial year valued at more than $42,000.

"Where inadvertent personal expenses are incurred, they must be repaid within one working day of the member becoming aware of the accidental use," an AFP spokesperson said.

Employees at the Health Department accumulated about $5,370 in accidental private purchases in the 2025-26 financial year.

A spokesperson for the department said it undertook compliance reviews and that cardholders cannot withdraw cash from their credit cards.

Labor puts squeeze on public service After it campaigned against a Coalition pledge to cut 41,000 public servants, Labor is ramping up its own efficiency drive.

The Department of Employment and Workplace Relations also recorded $8,688 in inadvertent personal purchases, with all of them repaid.

At the Department of Social Services, $2,250 in accidental personal purchases on work credit cards were paid back.

Both the employment and social services departments noted personal purchases were banned on work-issued credit cards.

The Department of Defence meanwhile recorded 3,276 purchases valued at about $240,000 that it described as "contrary to Defence policy".

The department has confirmed at least $213,672 of it has been paid back.

"Defence maintains a strong compliance and control framework to ensure inadvertent personal purchases are identified and addressed," a spokesperson said.

World.title: Peter Garrett on the one thing more valuable than success
World.content:
Midnight Oil never made noise for the sake of it.

Politically driven and socially conscious, the legendary Australian rock band always made music with meaning, reflecting what they saw to be the greatest global and local injustices.

Watch every episode of Take 5 with Zan Rowe right here Catch interviews with Shania Twain, David Byrne, Darren Hayes, Jacinda Ardern and more.

Frontman Peter Garrett's first exposure to protest music came early.

In his episode of ABC TV's Take 5 with Zan Rowe, he recalls hearing African American spiritual turned civil rights anthem Tell It on the Mountain by American folk trio Peter, Paul and Mary as a child.

"When these first protest records started coming out, my mum went out and bought them and started playing them endlessly," he says. "So, I could hear this from my bedroom and then I got to know it and understand it."

The young Garrett was unaware it was a protest song. As with so much great art, his understanding of the song and its importance grew over the years.

"When I listened to it again, I was really transported not only to the memory of listening as a kid, but also what that song then became for people," he says.

"I had an awareness of now. It gave the song extra weight for me."

The making of a frontman

It wasn't long before a young Peter Garrett was putting his own voice out there.

"I started in choirs and I really loved it," he says. "I was one of the only boys in the church choir up on the North Shore in Sydney."

Upon starting university in Canberra, Garrett leapt at the chance to take the lead role in one of the rock bands on campus.

"I'm not shy," he says. "I'm lucky. I don't have stage fright or anything like that. So, I didn't have to be urged. I was ready to go.

"It was a band called Devil's Breakfast. Probably the worst name. That's what we sounded like. We changed our name, thankfully, to Rock Island Line."

Peter Garrett fronts Midnight Oil at a triple j concert at Sydney's Capitol Theatre in March 1982. (ABC)

That band was short-lived, but Garrett had the bug. After leaving Canberra, he wasted no time in joining up with a new set of musicians.

"Eventually I came up to Sydney and fell in with this other bunch of young miscreants. Rob Hirst, Jim Moginie, and later Martin Rotsey, and, yeah, the rest was history," he says.

The outfit, Midnight Oil, blew up Australia's booming pub rock scene in the late 1970s thanks to songs that were as intense, urgent and energetic as their breathless live shows. In the 80s and 90s, they became a global force, troubling charts in the UK, US, Canada and Europe.

Midnight Oil's alchemy is hard to explain: this doco is a good start The career-spanning documentary makes a strong attempt to convey what makes Midnight Oil one of the world's most powerful rock bands.

Hindsight may be 20/20, but Garrett swears he felt the magic from the outset.

"When I first came in to meet them, Rob started playing and so did Jim, they were 17 or 18, and I just looked at them and I went, 'Wow,'" he says.

"Something in me just knew that this was very special. I never knew how far it would go."

While Garrett has often seemed the face and figurehead of Midnight Oil, powerhouse drummer Rob Hirst, who died of cancer earlier this year, was another force behind many of their most enduring songs.

"Rob and I competed with one another sometimes," Garrett says. "It's like having a frontman on the drums, who's also a great singer and a songwriter," he says.

"Always with respect. Pushing to try and always make it as good as we could."

Protest music's continued relevance

Those drawn to Midnight Oil's music and message commonly lament the lack of protest music making waves in the current day.

Loading Instagram content

But music with a message is still out there. For Garrett, the missives of Filipino and Murrawarri artist Dobby ring loudly.

He chooses the song Dirrpi Yuin Patjulinya for his Take 5, a highlight from Dobby's ARIA-winning 2024 concept album Warrangu: River Story, which outlines the cultural importance of the Bogan, Culgoa and Barwon Rivers, and the over-irrigation and water theft that plagues them.

"I share the deep call from the heart that he has about the Murray-Darling, about what we've done to our river systems," Garrett says.

"I still don't think that we've gotten to the point with leaders, with governments, where we deeply understand how important the natural world is to us and what we're doing to it. He absolutely sums it up here. It is epic."

Any perceived dearth of protest music shouldn't be too surprising. In a precarious career environment for creatives, there are risks to sticking one's neck out. What's more, writing effective protest songs is difficult.

"Part of the challenge … is to try and have that work in a song where people don't run away from it whilst at the same time not being too self-conscious about it," Garrett says.

"[Dobby] has done it in a way which is very powerful and without reservation. It's epic in a way, and it's going right to the heart of where things are at now in country."

Hear extended episodes of Take 5 right here Dive even deeper into the music that has inspired your favourite artists on the Take 5 podcast.

It's not just a young man's game.

At 76, Bruce Springsteen also knows how to make protest music that connects.

Garrett considers the live version of the Edwin Starr classic War, recorded in Minneapolis around the time of this year's ICE raids, particularly electric.

"Tonight, we ask all of you to join with us in choosing hope over fear, democracy over authoritarianism," Springsteen rages in his intro.

"The rule of law over lawlessness, ethics over unbridled corruption, resistance over complacency, unity over division, and peace over war."

For Garrett, this call is a clear example of the impact of protest music.

"The way he introduces this song, and the way that they play it, says everything to me about what we all need to do in this era that we live in," Garrett says.

"The fact that he can get up and say, in a highly polarised country, this is what the times demand, he's really risen to the moment.

"It sounds as strong and as fresh and as needed as it was when he first played it, and when it was first written. Powerful. Necessary."

What drives us

Protest music is often born from rage and frustration. But the strongest examples aren't defeatist: they are driven by hope.

Double J — a place for music lovers Double J gives you the new music you'll actually love, alongside the classic tracks you keep coming back to. Give your playlist a rest and join us here.

"Hope is realising there can be a better future through action," Garrett says. "Hope is the antidote to apathy and disinterest and cynicism.

"So, hope becomes the most important and precious commodity that we have, but not hope which is born of wishful thinking, hope that's born of an understanding that it is people who change the world. It's people acting that make the difference."

And Garrett considers hope for the future a more appealing prospect than nostalgia. Despite spending most of his 73 years as a rock star or federal politician, Garrett isn't one to dwell.

"I don't look back," he says. "It's great to yarn about it, but I don't spend much time meditating on the past.

" At my stage of the game, my most precious resource by far, apart from love and family and connection, is time. There's nothing that's more important to me now than that. "

Even when performing on the stage of Sydney's Hordern Pavilion at this year's APRA Awards in tribute to Hirst, Garrett knew he had to get the job done, lest the gravity of the situation overwhelm him.

"The legacy of the band, in terms of my experience of it, it takes up so much space in how I think and feel," he says.

"If you start to get too introspective about it, or if you're always looking in the rear-vision mirror, or even assessing what it is, you're buggered."

At 73, Peter Garrett says time is one of his most precious resources. (ABC: Jess Gleeson)

Garrett's performance that night was not born from protest, but from celebration. But the approach remains the same no matter the task at hand.

"You've just got to be in the moment," he says.

"It's not easy to do, but it is the key. Hang in the moment, make the moment work as best as you can, and then out the door."

Watch every episode of Take 5 with Zan Rowe right now on ABC iview.

Hear extended interviews with all guests on the Take 5 podcast.

World.title: Hugo Weaving’s compelling new Australian drama will leave you wanting more
World.content:
★★★★ CultureTV & radioReview Hugo Weaving’s compelling new Australian drama will leave you wanting more Craig Mathieson August 20, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Airport Chaplain ★★★★ I devoured the first four episodes of this new Australian drama. The individual instalments are not quite a half hour in length and that works all too well – any longer and the show’s inherent interest about how people and structures genuinely operate would become overwhelming. The Airport Chaplain has a thrilling sense of curiosity, for characters and organisations. It shows you enough to leave you wanting more, helping make it the timeliest Australian series in recent memory. Hugo Weaving and Claudia Karvan in The Airport Chaplain. As the fictional chaplain of Melbourne Airport, Tobias Wallace (Hugo Weaving) is the first responder of choice for the emotional, erratic and misplaced. Armed with empathy, vouchers, and intricate knowledge of the facility’s infrastructure, the old hand rushes from one pressing issue to the next, be it an unregistered support animal, a flight arriving with a passenger who has died onboard, or someone barricading themselves in the prayer room. “No, I’m not authorised,” Tobias will note, then carry on as if he is. Weaving suggests, without ever stressing the point, a myriad of qualities in Tobias, including the contradictory. Is he so determined to solve a problem that he creates more? Is he a humble aide or the possessor of a hero complex? Estranged from his own family, for reasons hinted at, Tobias is so dedicated to his unpredictable job that he appears to be living in a remote corner of the airport. He’s a people-first humanist lodged in a billion-dollar business. That’s tricky.



Editor's pick ★★

Review Hot priest? I wish! This holy love story will instead have you praying for a better script “Your role here is undefined,” his new boss, Terminal Manager Mira Ansari-Cole (Shabana Azeez), tells Tobias, bringing an end to his unsupervised pastoral care. A beacon of efficiency from a different generation and background than Tobias, Mira is at the pointy end of corporate growth – she’s being squeezed from above and defied from beneath, while her own domestic situation is plainly fraught. Tobias and Mira are wary of each other, sometimes adversarial, but there’s also a sense that perhaps they could help each other. The Airport Chaplain was created by Elise McCredie (Stateless) and Jude Troy (The Clearing). The storytelling has a sense of people and place that feels authentic – the bustle and friction is perpetual. The airport is a living organism, complete with a black economy, undocumented favour bank and anthropological edges. The first time Mira tries to make demands of the lead baggage handler, Lex Pascoe (Erroll Shand), he explodes with pent-up complaints about the substandard work conditions his subterranean crew endures. Shabana Azeez as airport manager Mira Ansari-Cole in The Airport Chaplain. There has been a slew of reality series about airport terminal chaos, but in this setting every day brings new issues: don’t get rostered on Valentine’s Day, do help the fearful wife trying to get on a flight before her abusive husband finds her. But in a broader, unspoken way, The Airport Chaplain is about how things work at scale in Australia, and the individuals who influence them. The theoretical and the practical are constantly at odds, as are people and profits.

World.title: The 30 best movies to stream on Disney+ right now
World.content:
10 Things I Hate About You, starring Heath Ledger and Julia Stiles.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The chills of winter demand a night in with a great movie. The problem? Choice paralysis. Every streaming platform has thousands of films available. To cut through that, here are 30 great hand-picked movies on Disney+ right now. Related Article Streaming The best 30 movies to stream on Amazon Prime Video right now Don’t have Disney+? Check out our guides on Stan*, HBO Max, Netflix and Amazon Prime Video. 10 Things I Hate About You (1999) Heath Ledger arrived in Hollywood with this quick-witted American high school take on Shakespeare’s The Taming of the Shrew, playing the rebel who falls for Julia Stiles’s antisocial classmate after being paid to date her. Aliens (1986) The rare sequel – written and directed by James Cameron – that is just as good as its predecessor. Sigourney Weaver returns as the lone survivor, with the science-fiction setting switching from horror to furious Xenomorph action.



Andrew Scott and Paul Mescal in All of Us Strangers. Parisa Taghizadeh/Searchlight Pictures All of Us Strangers (2023) A beautifully bittersweet invocation from Andrew Haigh, this London-set romantic fantasy stars Andrew Scott and Paul Mescal as marooned high-rise neighbours whose connection transcends time and loss. The Avengers (2012) Marvel’s original superhero team-up remains the genre’s benchmark, with Joss Whedon helming a drily bemused campaign to save the world that gave purposeful roles to the likes of Robert Downey Jr, Chris Evans and Scarlett Johansson. Colin Farrell and Brendan Gleeson in The Banshees of Inisherin. Searchlight Pictures The Banshees of Inisherin (2022)



On a remote Irish island in 1923, the friendship shared by Brendan Gleeson and Colin Farrell’s characters is unilaterally severed by the former, bewildering the latter. Absurdist humour and bloody ramifications ensue. Black Panther (2018) A true masterpiece of the Marvel age. Ryan Coogler’s African epic is rich in anthropological detail, thrilling action and the tragic rivalry between Chadwick Boseman’s titular superhero and Michal B. Jordan’s ruthless usurper. Chadwick Boseman was the star of Black Panther. AP Broadcast News (1987) The apex of the sophisticated Hollywood romantic-comedy, with writer and director James L. Brooks charting a memorable love triangle between William Hurt’s charming correspondent, Holly Hunter’s driven news producer and Albert Brooks’ yearning pal. Con Air (1997)



A bonkers action-thriller pitting the likes of Nicolas Cage, Nicolas Cage’s mullet, John Malkovich, and – yes – John Cusack against each other. This airborne jailbreak is so over the top it acquires a screw-loose charm. Nicolas Cage in Con Air. Dawn of the Planet of the Apes (2014) Prior to The Batman, filmmaker Matt Reeves announced himself with a compelling entry in this science-fiction saga that charts revolutionary compromise as apes and humans try to share a post-apocalyptic world. The Descendants (2011) With George Clooney and a young Shailene Woodley expertly matched as a father and defiant daughter dealing with a tragic mutual loss, this Alexander Payne tragicomedy explores familial forgiveness through messy circumstances and eloquent acceptance. Action flick or Christmas classic? Bruce Willis as John McClane in Die Hard. 20th Century Fox



Die Hard (1988) With a barefoot and bloodied Bruce Willis defying Alan Rickman’s suave terrorist and his dedicated crew, this landmark action-thriller is a treat. The action goes vertical as a skyscraper is filled with gunfire and sardonic dialogue. Ed Wood (1994) Tim Burton is at his most compassionate in this tragicomic homage to the titular 1950s director judged by history as Hollywood’s worst. A zesty Johnny Depp embodies Wood’s enthusiasm, with Martin Landau as a screen legend fallen on hard times. Darth Vader (David Prowse), Lando Calrissian (Billy Dee Williams) and Boba Fett (Jeremy Bulloch) in The Empire Strikes Back. Lucasfilm The Empire Strikes Back (1980) It’s still the best Star Wars movie. The adolescent heroics of George Lucas’ blockbuster space opera become a darkly powerful and resonant fable of family, faith, and looming doom.

World.title: Enough with the boring alpha men, this is the TV trend I can’t get enough of
World.content:
CultureMoviesThe Verdict Opinion Enough with the boring alpha men, this is the TV trend I can’t get enough of Paul Kalina Contributor August 20, 2026 — 5:30am

August 20, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ride or Die, Prime Video’s new eight-part series starring Hannah Waddingham and Octavia Spencer, is loud, silly, funny, escapist and as moreish as the popcorn that it deserves to be paired with. Since when does a show about people who kill for a living have the right to be so enjoyable? Maybe since posturing, humourless and amoral sharpshooter men, ostensibly saving the world from bad guys, passed the baton – and their weapons – to their female counterparts. May all our TV assassins be wise-cracking, arse-kicking women of a certain age. Sydney Morning Herald The premise here is that Judith Burton (Waddingham) has led a secret life for 20-plus years as a professional assassin, codenamed Whiptail, for an MI6-type spy outfit. It’s a secret that not even her bestie, Debbie (Octavia Spencer), has any inkling of. This is despite their ability to finish each other’s sentences, correctly guess if a contestant on Antiques Roadshow owns trash or treasure, and rescue each other from sanctimonious snobs at their weekly book club. While Whiptail has kept her shadow life secret (“I kill people for a living,” she finally blurts out), Debbie, who is American, has spent the past 20 years of hers raising children and steering the political career of her dimwit husband (Jamie Parker). That is, until her wet-eared husband, who is on the cusp of becoming the next prime minister, casually reveals he’s divorcing her and has taken money from the kinds of people that Whiptail hunts down.



After a hit gone wrong, Whiptail is handed an assignment to redeem herself and, before you know it, Debbie and Whiptail are dodging bullets and Albanian mobsters, having deep and meaningful conversations about their friendship and trying to find the bad guys who want to take them out, which involves numerous shootouts across a range of glamorous, postcard-perfect European backdrops and guilt-free trysts with younger men. Hannah Waddingham and Octavia Spencer (with Ed Skrein) in Ride or Die. Along with her immaculate wardrobe and coiffure, Waddingham infuses her character with sass, brassiness and sly humour. “Where’s the showmanship?” she asks when instructed to poison her next target. Debbie, who really is the smartest person in the room, never misses the chance for a throwaway quip and to serve comeuppance to anyone who doubts her. And behind the humour and cartoony spectacle there’s the burning indignation of two women who have been underestimated, disregarded and mistreated, and won’t be bound by social and marital expectations. “You’re a WOACA – you turned 50 and started acting out,” Whiptail’s insipid young handler tells her in a tone that suggests that’s a problem.



Understandably, Ride or Die is frequently compared to Killing Eve, the groundbreaking thriller co-created by Phoebe Waller-Bridge and Emerald Fennell (among others) that aired between 2018 and 2022. There, Jodie Comer played a ruthless and wonderfully demented psychopath named Villanelle who works for a secret organisation named The Twelve and becomes the singular obsession of intelligence officer Eve Polastri, played by Sandra Oh. Like Judith/Whiptail, Villanelle was raised in an orphanage (a key selection criterion for TV serial killers and assassins), has a dazzling wardrobe, insatiable taste for luxury (despite her humble beginnings) and complete indifference for authority figures, males in particular. Both shows pivot on the relationships between women bound by a mutual cause and a magnetic bond. Keira Knightley popping off in Black Doves. Netflix via AP The most memorable bits of the otherwise disposable Netflix thriller Black Doves also involves female assassins who are in possession of darkly comic streaks. The plot is largely incoherent and overblown – something about a murdered Chinese ambassador and his missing daughter, nuclear armaments and deep state operatives – but it’s mostly saved by Keira Knightley’s comic-book turn as a sharpshooting spy who is married to Britain’s defence secretary. One minute she’s hosting a posh Christmas party in her Belgravia pile and tucking the kids into bed, the next she’s wiping blood spatter off her face. And that’s before a pair of hilarious, trigger-happy lesbian mercenaries, played by Gabrielle Creevy and Ella Lily Hyland, become involved. If a spin-off isn’t in the works, it should be.



The humorous tone of both Ride or Die and Black Doves is more consistent and omnipresent than it is in The Assassin (Stan). Here Keeley Hawes plays the title role as the middle-aged woman whose sinister past has caught up with her. Related Article The Verdict The most underrated film of the 21st century? It’s nice, guys She’s retired from her role as a gun-for-hire, and living on a Greek island. Then a visit from her estranged son Edward (Freddie Highmore), hoping for a rapprochement, kicks off what ultimately turns out to be a formulaic shoot-em-up thriller. There are glimpses of black comedy as Hawes’ no-nonsense and reckless Julie reveals her deficit of maternal instincts and tries to bond with her meek and introspective son, but it’s not long before this is overshadowed by testosterone-fuelled bloodbaths and acrobatic violence sequences.

World.title: ‘It’s a really intense experience’: The reality show that’s more like a ‘therapy session’
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Robert Wellington, associate professor of art history at the Australian National University, was first contacted about being a judge on the ABC’s Portrait Artist of the Year, he thought it was a scam. “Strangely, they found me on LinkedIn of all places,” he says. “I thought the whole thing was a hoax. I thought it was a big ad and I was about to get charged for LinkedIn Premium or something, but no, it turned out to be legit.” His fellow judge, award-winning multidisciplinary artist Abdul Abdullah, couldn’t believe it either. “I was always a massive fan of the British program,” he says of Sky Arts’ Artist of the Year, which began in 2013. “When I was contacted to be a part of the show I was really, really, really excited and just wanted to be involved in whatever capacity. To be a judge, it is such a joy. It’s the dream job I didn’t know was possible.” Portrait Artist of the Year hosts Luke McGregor and Miranda Tapsell, with judges Robert Wellington, Bree Pickering and Abdul Abdullah. With their judging colleague, director of the National Portrait Gallery Bree Pickering, the three return for Portrait Artist of the Year’s second year, hosted again by actor Miranda Tapsell and comedian Luke McGregor. The judges must find a winner from 54 entrants, a mix of emerging, amateur and professional artists of all ages and backgrounds who, each have four hours to create a portrait of a well-known person who arrives minutes before the clock starts.



Some of the artists use oils, charcoal or soft pastels; other sear into their canvas with a blowtorch or brush gouache across a camping swag or sprinkle salt crystals into their paint to trigger star-like explosions in the background. All are fairly gobsmacked to be selected from the hundreds who apply to compete for a portrait commission that will hang in the National Portrait Gallery. Related Article Australian TV There’s no more Mother and Son, but Denise Scott has found a new path to travel “What is beautiful about the show is it shows you an artist at work,” Pickering says. “We have to remember that behind every art work is a person pouring their skill and their inner worlds out into the public, and for the public to judge and hopefully enjoy.” In 2026, the portrait-sitters range from country music star Troy Cassar-Daley to singer and TV personality Dannii Minogue, broadcaster Carrie Bickmore, food writer and presenter Matt Preston, filmmaker, author and radio presenter John Safran, radio, TV and podcast presenter Kate Langbroek and 2026 Australian of the Year and space engineer and astronaut Katherine Bennell-Pegg, among others. Judge Bree Pickering watches artist Cherie Ceberano at work in season two of Portrait Artist of the Year. Besides the pressure on each artist, it is common for the show’s sitters to express great emotions once they view their finished portrait. “It’s a really intense experience,” Wellington says. “The sitter’s on the little stage for four hours, the judges are scrutinising the works, the artists are scrutinising the sitters. There’s cameras everywhere and they’re being asked personal questions.



“They’ve brought a special object with them and often the object carries a really powerful story about their lives, maybe about a relative that’s passed, or it evokes something very powerful to their own origin story. “It’s like a therapy session. An attachment grows between the sitter and artist. So, when the portrait is turned and shown it’s like a crescendo and all of those emotions of the day come out. It’s a perfect storm for creating that kind of emotional response.” Judge Abdul Abdullah chats to artist Jarrod Prince in Portrait Artist of the Year. Like any TV awards show, winning comes with a caveat: victory does not ensure future success. But that’s not the point. “Not many people can make such a commercial success of their practice that they can live off it,” Wellington says. “That’s a really exceptional thing, particularly in Australia, but probably anywhere in the world. “But choosing to have a life of arts practice or to have art practice in your life is something we can all do. The show reveals how broad our artistic community in Australia is, how many people are spending a lot of time practising and honing their skills who may not have other avenues to show people what they’re doing. This show does give them another avenue, which is really, really precious.” Wellington, Pickering and Abdullah are also extremely conscious of the responsibilities that come with being a judge.



“In all areas of our work we are constantly tussling with each other over what we like,” Pickering says. “A new art movement comes forward, and we’re like, ‘Oh, that’s a bit challenging’, ‘That’s a bit new. We don’t like that’. Related Article Opinion

Australian TV If you are still complaining about Australian TV, it’s time to shut up Louise Rugendyke National TV editor “That’s been the history of art. We all love talking about how modernism changed everything and people hated it when it first came out. It’s part of the beauty of the creative process over time and the show celebrates that.” Abdullah agrees. “The judging part is really difficult,” Abdullah says. “But one of the most valuable things is how the show brings art and the joy of art-making to a new audience. “I have had so many conversations with people who aren’t otherwise gallery-goers or art connoisseurs and they’re rapt with the program and going on this journey with this artist. The more people that like art or are exposed to art, the better.” Wellington, known for his work specialising in the art of France in the 17th and 18th centuries and for wearing fabulous Vivienne Westwood outfits, recalls his first introduction to art.



“I don’t come from a particularly arty or privileged background and my access point to art and culture was through TV shows like [by] my beloved Sister Wendy Beckett,” he says of the late British nun and presenter of popular BBC art documentaries in the 1990s. Portait sitter Kate Langbroek with host Luke McGregor on Portrait Artist of the Year. “Seeing her on television, a great eccentric and wonderful access to art was amazing. “If we can’t be out there being passionate and talking about works of art, there’s going to be a whole generation of kids who don’t get to see it, who don’t get that little light turned on and think, ‘Oh, hang on a minute, there’s something else out there for me’. Related Article ★★★★

Review Hugo Weaving’s compelling new Australian drama will leave you wanting more “This is showing people we’re passionate and that this is a world for them. It’s not exclusive. Art is for anyone who wants to join.” Portrait Artist of the Year airs at 7.30pm on Sundays on the ABC and is streaming on ABC iview.

World.title: ASX set to inch up, Wall Street higher as US flags bond buyback; Moderna rockets after cancer vaccine trial results
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to inch up, Wall Street higher as US flags bond buyback; Moderna shares rocket after cancer vaccine study results Stan Choe August 20, 2026 — 5:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks are ticking higher after the US Treasury Department said it will buy more US government bonds in a move that eased pressure on financial markets worldwide. Strong profit reports for the spring from Estee Lauder, Target and other US companies are also helping to support the stock market. The S&P 500 rose 0.3 per cent and is on track for its first gain in four days after setting its all-time high last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 133 points, or 0.3 per cent, as of 2:30 p.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was up 0.2 per cent. Wall Street notched another winning week. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to edge higher, with futures at 5am AEST pointing to a rise of 13 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX fell for a sixth-straight session on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US71.24¢. A busy day on the reporting season calendar is ahead, with and Northern Star among companies due up. The stock market has been under growing strain as worries about inflation, big government debts and other factors drive Treasury yields higher in the bond market. That ultimately makes borrowing money more expensive for everyone, which slows the economy and undercuts prices for stocks and other investments.



Related Article Analysis

Home loans Five charts that explain what’s really happening with housing But Treasury yields fell in the morning after the US Treasury Department said it will at least double the size of its planned purchases of longer-term Treasurys from September 9 through November 4. The department said it’s doing so “to provide greater liquidity support in longer-dated nominal sectors where there is consistent strong sponsorship from market participants.” These longer-term 10- and 30-year Treasurys are less beholden to the Federal Reserve, which can raise or lower very short-term interest rates for overnight loans. President Donald Trump has lobbied for the Fed to lower interest rates to help the economy. Instead, longer-term yields are set by investors in the bond market, who are deciding how much interest they need to get paid by the US government in exchange for lending it money. And recently, they have been demanding more in interest to make up for the growing risks of high inflation, continued government deficits and other factors. After the Treasury department’s announcement, the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.66 per cent from 4.71 per cent late Tuesday. It, though, remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran sent oil prices and worries about inflation much higher.



The 30-year Treasury yield, which has recently touched its highest level since 2007, fell more sharply to 5.2 per cent from 5.28 per cent late Tuesday. On Wall Street, Moderna and Merck helped lead the market after they announced encouraging initial results from a study of a cancer vaccine they co-developed. The new drug showed better recurrence-free survival in melanoma patients who had a combination of it and Keytruda, a prescription immunotherapy drug made by Merck, than with Keytruda alone. Moderna soared 138.4 per cent, while Merck jumped 12.4 per cent. The continuing parade of US companies to report bigger profits for the spring than analysts expected, meanwhile, continues to support stocks. Estee Lauder rallied 17.4 per cent after CEO Stéphane de La Faverie said a key measure of its revenue growth accelerated for a fourth straight quarter. It reported growth in revenue around the world, with the strongest in mainland China.



The skin care company reported earnings per share of 39 cents, after excluding some restructuring and other one-time expenses. That’s up from just 9 cents a year earlier and was better than the 32 cents that analysts expected, according to FactSet. Related Article Opinion

Retail Retailers on the ropes as consumers all but close their wallets Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Such growth is imperative because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term. And strong growth helps allay criticism that stock prices shot too high in their runs to records. Target rose 5.9 per cent, Lowe’s added 2.8 per cent and homebuilder Toll Brothers climbed 5.3 per cent after they all also reported better profits for the latest quarter than expected. They helped offset drops for some Big Tech stocks, which restrained the overall market. Broadcom fell 4.3 per cent, for example, and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. It and other winners of the artificial-intelligence boom have been swinging sharply through the summer on worries that their stocks may have shot too high and that the AI frenzy may not be sustainable if it doesn’t produce big-enough profits.



In stock markets abroad, indexes were mostly lower in Asia and mixed in Europe. Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 sank 3.2 per cent. South Korea’s Kospi, which has been home to some of the world’s sharpest swings because of its heavy reliance on AI stocks, slumped 5.8 per cent.
