That included research in 2024 that found more preschoolers ended up in New Zealand hospitals on hot days.

Children, older people and those with existing health conditions were all vulnerable to heat, he said.

"Many of the main chronic health issues - things like cardiovascular disease, respiratory disease, psychiatric problems - many of these things are sensitive to heat in the short term, so you see increases in hospital admissions and deaths from those things."

Heatwaves are defined as several consecutive days where temperatures fall in the top few percent of what is considered normal for that time and place.

"It's a little bit hard to understand at first glance," Hales said.

"If you take the example of a city that's in the north of Europe, people might start to have an increase in the health effects of heat at temperatures that we would consider to be quite comfortable," he said.

"Likewise, people who live in tropical countries probably would not have any effect on their health at temperatures that we would start to be thinking, 'this is getting pretty hot'."

The preparation for future hot weather in New Zealand was "lagging a bit, but it's not disastrous".

"The more important question is, how's our preparation for [mitigating] climate change at the moment? And I would give you a very different answer to that question - I think, as a country, we are going backwards."

Children playing at the splash pad at Māngere’s Moana-Nui-ā-Kiwa Pools and Leisure centre. Supplied / Auckland Council

Green space, building design provide possible solutions

Simpson said creating more green space in urban areas could both mitigate climate change and help cities adapt to it.

"Not only do trees and plants help to cool our urban environment, but they provide a myriad of other benefits - from supporting our biodiversity, stormwater management, improving the aesthetics and connection for people with nature, and absorbing or sequestering carbon."

There were additional things to consider in urban planning and development, such as using building and paving materials that reflected heat instead of absorbing it.

That included thinking about how homes were built, she said.

"In recent times we've made quite a good shift to making our homes warmer and drier. We now need to be thinking about making them cooler."

Last year, Auckland Council and the New Zealand Green Building Council (NZGBC) sent a joint letter to the government asking for changes to the Building Code, requiring new houses to pass a check at the design stage to ensure they would not overheat.

NZGBC chief executive Andrew Eagles said half of new builds now were terrace houses and apartments, and many of them were overheating too frequently.

"We don't recess our windows, so you're not shading that space. And at the same time we've had a love affair with very large glazing - and that so the combination of large glazing and no cross-ventilation and not recessing means the house just can't get rid of all that heat."

Many designs would require only minor tweaks, such as slightly smaller windows - which would save money too - and larger eaves, he said.

"It's all things that can be manageable, but if you don't have to do that check then the home is going to overheat for large parts of January, February, March, causing really significant discomfort."

With the right design, it was possible to have a home that was both warm in winter and cool in summer, Eagles said.

World.title: CNMI leader urges caution as US advances Pacific seabed mining plan
World.content:
The Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) Governor David Apatang says protecting Pacific waters and island communities must come first as the United States moves ahead with plans that could eventually open a vast area of seabed around the Mariana Trench to mineral development.

The US Marine Minerals Administration, formerly the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, has issued a proposed leasing notice which has triggered a 60-day review by the governor.

Apatang said his administration would approach the proposal with "extreme caution".

He said the territory wants safeguards in place before any final leasing decisions were made.

Apatang's administration is seeking independent, peer-reviewed environmental baseline studies, protections for commercial and subsistence fishing, local workforce development, port infrastructure investment, contracting opportunities for island businesses, and a role for Northern Marianas officials and traditional leaders in reviewing survey plans and monitoring data.

"We must ensure that no activity, survey or otherwise, takes place without rigorous scientific baseline studies, complete transparency, and explicit protections for our marine resources," Apatang said.

The proposal comes as seabed mining emerges as a wider Pacific issue, with governments and environmental groups across the region debating the potential economic benefits against risks to largely unexplored deep-sea ecosystems.

"We welcome dialogue with the Department of the Interior and the Marine Minerals Administration, but our priority remains unchanged," Apatang said.

"We will thoroughly examine the proposed terms over the next 60 days to ensure that the ecological integrity of our waters and the long-term well-being of the CNMI are fully safeguarded."

Advocate warns of 'permanent and irreversible risks'

Northern Marianas environmental advocate Angelo Villagomez, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, said the risks would be borne by Pacific Islanders while the economic rewards could flow elsewhere.

"Trump's attempt to mine the seabed of the Mariana Trench will only benefit far off corporate interests, while the people who call these islands home will be left with all the costs and none of the benefits," Villagomez said.

"Any damage that happens from mining in this area presents permanent and irreversible risks to fragile ecosystems."

The Center for American Progress said the Proposed Leasing Notice covers about 69 million acres of federal seabed surrounding the Mariana Trench, an area roughly the size of Nevada.

The proposed lease sale involves federal waters offshore the Mariana Islands and next to the Mariana Trench Marine National Monument.

Villagomez also accused the US administration of ignoring opposition from island communities and local governments.

"The administration is again ignoring the overwhelming concerns voiced by the people and local governments," he said.

The Center for American Progress said about 60,000 public comments were submitted before the Proposed Leasing Notice was issued. Its release also cited Apatang as telling AFP earlier this month: "There have been no consultations with the people of the Northern Mariana Islands."

World.title: West Papua issue likely to be on agenda in Palau - PNG foreign minister
World.content:
Papua New Guinea's foreign minister says he expects the issue of West Papua will be discussed at the upcoming Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) leaders meeting in Palau.

This comes as the issue of human rights abuses and conflict in Indonesian-ruled Papua region, often known internationally as West Papua, appeared to have slipped off the regional agenda.

After the PIF foreign ministers met in Suva earlier this month, there was no mention of West Papua in the meeting's outcome statement.

Most of the talk was about regional security arrangements and the region's response, or lack thereof, to a recent Chinese nuclear-capable interballistic missile test into Pacific waters.

But PNG's Foreign Minister Justin Tkatchenko has indicated to RNZ Pacific that the West Papua issue will be discussed by Pacific leaders in Koror next month.

Papua New Guinea APEC minister Justin Tkatchenko standing infront of APEC House in Port Moresby. RNZ / Koroi Hawkins

This is despite little to no apparent progress after Forum leaders last year tasked the Forum Secretariat to work constructively with Indonesia on a proposed visit to West Papua by PIF leaders envoys in 2026, in consultation with the Melanesian Spearhead Group (MSG) Secretariat

Tkatchenko denied that Indonesia had stalled progress on a proposed visit by Forum leaders envoys to West Papua.

"No, I don't think [Indonesia had stalled progress] at all," he said.

"Indonesia is very open to the situation now. I think it's just making a time and date and making it happen. I'm sure it can be brought up in the next meeting in Palau by the leaders, and if they need to work on that, so be it."

However, there has been a clear lack of action on a PIF resolution in 2019 to request Indonesia grant access to West Papua for the UN Human Rights Commissioner to come and look into alleged abuses.

Tkatchenko said Indonesia's government under new President Prabowo Subianto has been open about Papua issues.

However, he said the escalating violent conflict between Indonesian military and West Papuan independence fighters in recent months had not came up for discussion in Suva.

The West Papua National Liberation Army, or TPNPB, claimed responsibility for killing American pilot Nicholas F Gosselin after he landed a small aircraft in remote Sobaham District, Yahukimo Regency , in early July 2026 Supplied

"Well nothing was mentioned at the Pacific Island Forum Foreign Ministers Meeting in that regard, but I did make it clear that we respect the sovereignty of Indonesia, and we did elevate them for the leaders to ensure that Indonesia was in a strategic relationship with all Pacific Island Forum's members."

The foreign minister suggested Indonesia's role at the Forum could be a growing one, "as they hold 20 million Melanesians in Indonesia, which is bigger than all of the Pacific Islands and us put together".

"So, they hold a very important place when it comes to the representation of Melanesians in the whole of the Pacific, and especially in the Pacific Island Forum. So, that was put forward and mentioned, and the leaders will discuss that in Palau in the next coming weeks."

West Papuans protested in numerous cities and towns on 15 August 2026 to mark the anniversary of 1962's New York Agreement. Supplied

PNG relationship with Indonesia

Tkatchenko said from a PNG perspective, they have made it clear to their neighbour that they are willing to help Indonesia address its problems in Papua, if they'd like help.

"And we have the indications through the new president of Indonesia and the Foreign Minister's discussions with myself that things are moving forward for the betterment of West Papuans now and into the future.

The PNG minister was reluctant to point fingers at Indonesia over the unrest in its Papuan provinces, particularly Highland Papua.

"We have our own issues, too. I mean, we've had massacres and very unfortunate tribal wars and conflicts between our own people in the Highlands of Papua New Guinea that would equal or outdo what is happening in Indonesia.

"So we have our own law and order problems that we are also trying to address in that regard.

Indonesia's President Prabowo Subianto has deployed an increasing number of troops to Papua region. BAY ISMOYO/AFP

"But any human rights violation, of course, is always a worry, depending on what the circumstance is. And you know, they are our brothers and sisters, and we are concerned. And if the Indonesians need our assistance, so be it."

Pacific Islands Forum leaders are due to meet in Palau at the start of September.

Cross border help

Meanwhile, Tkatchenko said PNG Foreign Affairs officials had been in Jakarta finalising a cross-border treaty, which allows for help to PNG's Ok Tedi mine in Western Province near the international border.

"The Ok Tedi mine at the moment's in a bit of strife where the river has now basically dried up and has now gone from a river to a creek. So, the freight, bringing all the freight and goods and fuel to Ok Tedi has now ceased because of the river not being able to access proper water depths to flow the boats and barges up to the appropriate points.

"We have now got a road going through and bridges going through Indonesia for them to access fuel and goods and everything in from Indonesia.

World.title: 'There's been a slip': Inside the final hours before the fatal Mt Maunganui landslide
World.content:
A damning review into the fatal Mount Maunganui landslide details how one of the six victims went to extraordinary lengths to warn and help fellow campers before she was killed. National Crime Correspondent Sam Sherwood reports.

It was day three of what was a "spur of the moment" decision by Morrinsville teacher Lisa Maclennan and her husband Travis to spend a few nights at the Beachside Holiday Park in Mount Maunganui.

They still had one more night booked, but after being woken by a slope coming down behind their campervan at about 4.30am, the couple spent the next several hours helping fellow campers and trying to alert others before deciding, at about 8.30am, that they wanted to leave.

About 9:15am, after emptying the campervan toilet receptacle, Lisa Maclennan went to have a shower in the amenities block.

Also staying at the campground were 15-year-olds Sharon Maccanico and her boyfriend Max Furse-Kee. The couple had travelled with Maccanico's parents.

Maccanico's parents had initially decided to cut the holiday short two days in following some strong windows with heavy rain predicted. However, when Maccanico's father went to cancel the remainder of their booking he was encouraged by a member of the office to stay and said they had the option of renting a caravan or a cabin.

The family decided to rent a caravan to stay in until the storm passed, when they would return to their tent.

On the morning of 22 January, the sky was blue and the family had chosen a new campsite and were ready to move.

Lisa Maclennan was one of the six people killed in a landslide at Mount Maunganui in January. NZ POLICE / SUPPLIED

Shortly before 9:30am, Maccanico and Furse-Kee went off to the amenities block to have showers.

Minutes later, a large landslide came down, hitting about 30 campsites and engulfing the amenities block which included toilets, showers and laundry facilities.

Six people were killed. They were Maclennan, Maccanico, Furse-Kee and three others who were also in the amenities block, Susan Knowles, Jacqualine Wheeler and Måns Loke Bernhardsson.

On Wednesday, an external review by retired high court judge Hon Paul Davison KSO KC, commissioned by the Tauranga City Council, was released.

The report said information identifying a risk to life was received, filed, discussed, forwarded - and then left.

"The failure was not the fault of any one person; it was the failure of a system that enabled an identified risk to life to remain unowned, un-escalated and unmanaged."

Also inside the 268-page report lies details about the "heroic lengths" Maclennan took to help those around her.

The 'spur of the moment' trip

The Maclennans arrived at the Beachside Holiday Park in the campervan they had borrowed from Lisa's family on 20 January.

At 11.57am the following day, Travis received a Civil Defence Emergency Alert on his phone.

The alert told Travis that MetService had issued a red severe rain warning for Bay of Plenty from 9am to 9am the following day.

"Put safety first. Don't take any chances. Act quickly if you see rising water. Do not try to walk, swim, or drive in floodwater.

"Avoid all non-essential travel. Bring pets indoors and move livestock to high ground where possible."

The alert also said to "be prepared to evacuate".

After returning to the campground that afternoon they remained in the campervan for the night.

About 4.30am on 22 January, Lisa woke up after hearing a noise and feeling the campervan move, the report said.

"She woke Travis who says that Lisa was panicking and initially thought that it was an earthquake.

"She went out and saw that the slope behind the campervan had come down and hit the rear of their vehicle. Some of the mud and soil from the slip had gone under the campervan covering the electric cable which was connected to a power bollard."

Lisa Maclennan, pictured with her husband Travis. NZ POLICE / SUPPLIED

Lisa moved the campervan and then woke the people who were in a blue tent that was beside them as she was worried they could be trapped if any more of the slope failed.

The report said the Maclennans wanted to "urgently" contact the management of the holiday park to tell them what had happened "so that other campers would be alerted to the risk of any further slope failures".

At 4.43am, Travis called the numbers printed on the holiday park information sheet.

The call was initially answered by a security firm who transferred him to the Tauranga City Council (TCC) contact centre.

A transcript of the call said Travis told them they were staying at the holiday park and that they were trying to get hold of them.

"There's been a slip where we're staying, and it's affected a few of us, and we obviously don't know.

"Well, we want to get hold of them so that we can let them know, but it's affected a few people here…"

He added that "a few people here need to be relocated".

The contact centre staffer asked Travis if he had tried the intercom which should put him straight to the cellphone of a person whose name is redacted in the report and named Staff Member Q.

He replied he hadn't as they were "a little bit flustered, so we rang straight through to the number, and it put us straight through to you guys".

The staffer put Travis on hold and made two calls to the campground's after-hours number, however neither call was answered.

At 4.52am the staffer called the Emergency Management Officer's (EMO) phone and spoke to a Staff Member B and transferred Travis' call to her.

Travis told Staff Member B about the slip that had come down. He said they had found the intercom which they were going to use. Staff Member B said she would get someone to call them back.

At 5.15am, Staff Member B emailed the TCC Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) operations, welfare and intelligence to tell them about two phone calls she'd had.

One was about a call she'd had from police about a slip that had taken down a house on Waitaha Road with a 10-year-old and 70-year-old missing.

The other was from Travis. She detailed what he had told her and said she'd told him she would get someone to call him back.

The report said that after his call with Staff Member B, the Maclennans tried the intercom and knocked on the walls of the campground office but had no luck.

Officials work at the scene of the landslide at the Beachside Holiday Park in Mt Maunganui on 22 January 2026. Alan Gibson / Gibson Images Ltd

They then noticed that another landslip had come down further along the driveway towards two cabins.

The couple woke the occupants of the cabins, as well as some people who were in a campervan nearby.

At 5.21am Staff Member C, who was on duty supporting the EOC controller, called Travis.

In the EOC welfare log she noted the conversation and said Travis indicated he was assisting a neighbouring camper to move their belongings.

"There had been no injuries and Travis had a location in the campground that was appropriate to shelter in place until he could raise assistance from a staff member.

"Travis was advised to call back on the EOC welfare number should he need any further support. No further calls from Travis by 7am handover."

The 111 call

The report says that at 5.47am a local resident (referred to as Member of the Public A), who had been walking near the mountain, called 111 after seeing two large landslides had come down on the ocean side near the surf club building.

His call was transferred to Fire and Emergency (FENZ) who told him that landslides were a council matter and that FENZ would notify them.

A FENZ staffer then called the TCC contact centre and told Staff Member A that they had been informed that there had been a landslide at the bottom of the mountain.

The caller had "mentioned about potentially having some problems at the Holiday Park, if the weather continues".

Member of the Public A went to the surf club to tell the lifeguards about the landslides and started waking some campers.

Staff Member A called Staff Member D, whose responsibilities included the maintenance and repair of the walkways and tracks on Mauao. He then called Staff Member F and they made a decision to immediately close all public access points onto the mountain.

Staff Member D then drove to the campground.

The Maclennans returned to the campground office several times between 5.30am and 7am to try to find someone to tell about the slips. By now, three landslips from the slope above and behind their campervan had come down.

The report said the couple also spoke with other campers.

"Travis Maclennan recalls that while he and Lisa were concerned about what had happened and thought that other campers near the base of the mountain should be warned and moved, there was no panicking."

By dawn, other campers gathered around and the couple told them why they had moved their campervan.

The couple took several photos of the slips and the blue tent, the earliest was about 6.16am.

A photograph taken by Lisa Maclennan at 6.17am on January 22. supplied

'Major slip on mount'

At 6.40am, Staff Member J, who had been alerted to the landslide by Staff Member D, sent a message to a Teams chat group used by asset managers at TCC's City Operations and Spaces and Places team.

"Major slip on mount by camp site heading [there] now to meet [Staff Member D]".

The report also referred to a Staff Member Q, who started monitoring the weather on 21 January. About 4pm he received a call advising that heavy rainfall was forecast.

During the afternoon and evening he looked out for any flooding around the holiday park.

About 11pm he called a First Security staffer asking them to keep a look out for any flooding or damage.

"He told them to contact him if there was anything to report, regardless of the time."

About 6.30am on 22 January, he woke and checked the campground's beachfront CCTV camera on his phone and saw flooding all around the beachfront campsites.

Shortly after he got a call from TCC Call Centre and was told that City Operations and other TCC staff were out in front of the campground office.

Staff Member Q went over to the ocean beachfront to see the flooding and saw that a large slip had come down and covered the stone stairs and ramp that provided access from the campground up to the base track.

When Staff Member J arrived at the campground about 6.45am, he parked his vehicle near the office and put on a hi-vis jacket.

As he approached the office he saw some people knocking on the door.

The report said Lisa asked him if he was from the campground. He replied that he was from the council.

Staff Member J said his conversation with Lisa lasted "probably two minutes".

"He described her demeanour as being frustrated and agitated because she had not been able to get hold of anybody and there was no one from the campground around to speak to."

Local emergency services search for missing people following a landslide at Mount Maunganui in Tauranga on January 23, 2026. AFP / Ben Strang

He said Lisa told him that there was a "little slip" that had hit her caravan about 4.30am.

"She said that she was worried about the bank situation where her caravan was parked … [and that] she expressed concern that people around the base of the Mount should be evacuated."

Staff Member J said he told the Maclennans that he couldn't assist them, but he would try to contact the campground manager to tell him about their concerns.

"Staff Member J is clear that Lisa was not suggesting there was any need for an urgent response by the campground management, and she was not asking him to take any urgent action in relation to either the slips or the damage caused to their campervan."

After speaking to the couple he called Staff Member N and asked them to contact Staff Member Q and get someone down to the office.

Travis said that when he and Lisa saw Staff Member Q he was speaking to some campers.

He said his wife approached Staff Member Q and said he needed to come over to their side of the campground because there had been some slips there, and they had been trying to get hold of him all morning.

Travis alleged Staff Member Q responded with what the report describes as a "rather dismissive wave of his hand" saying "I'll get there when I get there".

The couple then went back to their campervan to wait for him.

Staff Member Q's version of the conversation was different. He said he was approached by four people while he was looking at the flooding around the ocean beach campsites.

He said the Maclennans told him their camper had a bit of damage to the rear bumper.

"I said as soon as I was finished, I would come over directly to see you."

A photograph taken by Lisa Maclennan at 8.01am. supplied

Maclennans check out

At 7.37am an email was sent to the TCC executive, including the CEO and his leadership team, as well as a councillor and three other people advising them that Mount Maunganui was being closed off.

"The storm event has damaged tracks, caused slips and downed trees that make it unsafe for the public to access.

"Thankfully, as far as we know, nobody got hurt during the event."

Staff Member Q turned up at the amenities block driving the campground golf cart about 7.40am, about 40 minutes after initially speaking to the Maclennans.

Staff Member J, who was in the golf cart with Staff Member Q, said as they approached the block on the golf cart, Lisa flagged them down.

"[Staff Member J] says that Lisa appeared very concerned and said that she had been warning people near the amenities block about the potential for further slips."

Travis said Staff Member Q had offered to refund their camping charges and replace the power cable which had been covered by the landslide, and that he would get it all sorted but was going to check the rest of the area first and then come back.

The report said the Maclennans and Staff Member Q had a "different understanding" of what Staff Member Q said he was going to do.

Travis said the couple waited for him to return as they "clearly understood" that he'd said he was going to come back after checking the rest of the camp. However, Staff Member Q said he told them he would meet them at reception.

The couple ended up giving up waiting and by 8.45am they had decided they were going to check out and leave.

Travis Maclennan said when they entered the office they were surprised to see Staff Member Q was there.

He gave the couple a refund for their camping charges and a replacement electric power cable.

Davison said in his report that by now "the storm had passed, the weather had cleared and the sun was out".

"It was another classic summer morning at the Mount."

A photograph taken by Lisa Maclennan at 8.08am. supplied

Tragedy strikes

The Maclennans arrived back at their campervan about 9am and decided they would have showers before they left. Travis had one first, when he returned Lisa said she wanted the campervan toilet receptacle emptied before they left.

Given her husband had just showered she said she would do it and then go have a shower.

"Having emptied the toilet receptacle, Lisa then went into the amenities block for her shower and Mr Maclennan waited for her in the campervan. It was then around 9.15am - 9.20am."

Furse-Kee and Maccanico's family were staying in a caravan right beside the Harbour Amenities block.

Maccanico's parents woke on the morning of 22 January about 7am. Sometime before 9am, Maccanico's mum spent about 30 minutes in the amenities block washing their dishes.

When she finished she went outside and saw her daughter and Furse-Kee standing near the caravan, the report said.

"Sharon asked for the keys so that they could use the showers, and after getting some clean clothes to change into, she and Max both went off into the amenities block to have showers.

"It was now only several minutes before 9.30am."

Davison said by 9.30am the storm of the past days was "well gone".

"Many campers had either left during or after the storm, or had moved away from the low-lying and flood-affected areas of the campground, and the campground was quieter than would be usual for that time of year.

"The campsites and the driveway along the top of the campground, beneath the slope of the mountain and beside the Harbour Amenities building, appeared largely empty."

Then, about 9.30am, the slope above the amenities block "failed without any obvious warning".

"A large mass of saturated soil, colluvium, rock and debris slid rapidly down the slope. Within seconds it had engulfed the amenities building.

"Staff around the campground heard the same thing first - a loud crack, variously described as thundering or an 'almighty roar' - and then saw the trees and slope sweep down onto and over the Harbour Amenities block and campsites below."

Davison said that family members of those trapped, other campers and members of the public and TCC staff "responded immediately and made frantic efforts to locate and rescue those trapped in the building".

"It was a chaotic scene as people arrived and desperately tried to locate anyone who had been caught in the landslide."

Davison said the TCC staff "without any hesitation put themselves in danger by going onto the landslide and making desperate efforts to locate and rescue those victims caught in, or trapped by, the landslide".

"Their conduct is justly characterised and commended as being undertaken with conspicuous bravery and humanity."

Retired high court judge Hon Paul Davison KSO KC. RNZ / Kim Baker Wilson

'Warnings came early and from several directions'

Among Davison's findings, he discussed the response on the morning of the landslide.

He said Travis' call nearly five hours before the landslide was handled as a welfare and accommodation matter, not as the report of a "geohazard requiring assessment of whether the affected area should be evacuated".

Davison said Staff Member Q had no Trigger Action Response Plan to inform his decision-making and alert him to the gravity of the situation.

He also said that neither Staff Member Q or his campground staff had received any training directed to the recognition of landslide precursors such as the seepage and flow from the toe of the slopes "as become increasingly obvious during the morning of 22 January".

Davison said he made no criticism of Staff Member Q or any of the TCC staff who were present at the campground on the morning of the landslide for not recognising the signs.

"The failure to take precautionary steps to evacuate everyone from the area around and below where the fatal landslide happened on the morning of 22 January was in essence deeply systemic in origin, and the consequence of an organisational structure and risk management process that had failed to capture the natural hazard landslide risk and ensure that it was effectively assessed and managed, despite the widespread knowledge held within the organisation regarding the existence of the risk and the means of effectively mitigating it."

In the report Davison said the "central conclusion of this review is sobering in its simplicity".

"This was not a hazard that was unknown, hidden, or beyond the reach of foresight.

"For more than two decades, one competent consultant after another identified the landslide hazard to the campground, located it on the very slope that failed, and explained - sometimes in stark terms - what the consequences of a landslide occurring could be."

The slip at Mauao, Mount Maunganui as seen from the air. Screengrab / Amy Till

Davison said on the morning of 22 January, these systematic flaws combined and were compounded.

"Warnings came early and from several directions."

This included from the intense rainfall, from the large slips already coming down around the mountain, from several smaller slips on the slope, and from muddy water streaming from the foot of the slope before it finally failed.

"The instinct to move people away from the toe of the slope was even voiced by some of those who observed these signs, but there was no plan against which to assess those warnings, no threshold criteria requiring action, and no training of staff enabling them to recognise observable signs which indicated an elevated risk of slope failure and no one charged with making a properly informed evacuation decision.

"The most consequential safety decision of that morning was left, by default, to the manager at the campground who have been given neither the tools nor the knowledge to make it.

"In my view, the criticism justly and appropriately lies with the organisation that left the campground manager and his staff so ill-equipped and unprepared to make the decisions that could have avoided this tragedy."

He said had a Trigger Action Response Plan of the kind been twice recommended, that morning would have looked very different.

Following the release of the review, Travis released a statement via police.

"The council report released [on Wednesday] highlights Lisa's extraordinary and selfless actions on the morning of the landslide.

World.title: Ruby Tui signs for English rugby club Trailfinders
World.content:
New Zealand rugby star Ruby Tui has signed a contract with England club Trailfinders.

Trailfinders, based in London suburb Ealing, hailed the signing, calling Tui "one of the most decorated and recognisable players in world rugby".

The BBC reported the contract was understood to be for a year.

Tui, 34, has had a huge impact in both sevens and 15s codes, playing a star role in the Black Ferns' Rugby World Cup victory in 2022 and being a gold medallist with the Black Ferns Sevens at the 2021 Tokyo Olympics, after winning silver at Rio in 2016.

She will join former Black Ferns teammate Alana Borland (nee Bremner) at Trailfinders, who made the final of the English premiership for the first time in June, but lost to Saracens 54-14.

Tui played for Chiefs Manawa in last year's Super Rugby Aupiki competition but missed out on selection for the Black Ferns squad chosen for last year's Rugby World Cup in England. She instead was a commentator at the Cup.

She has not had a contract since, but played for the Barbarians against Wales at Twickenham in June.

Trailfinders head coach Barney Maddison said Tui was one of the most respected figures in the women's game.

"Her experience of winning at the very highest level, combined with the energy and leadership she brings on and off the pitch, will be an enormous asset to the squad as we push on from last season. We're thrilled to welcome her to the club."

Tui told the club's website she was ''fizzing'' to sign with the club.

"I feel like I've seen a lot of women's rugby and it's the biggest and best women's comp in the world right now. The whole Trailfinders team have been so welcoming since I got here and watching them all last season had me fizzed about how they're playing the game."

Tui said it helped having a Kiwi presence in Borland at the club, while former teammates Tanya Kalounivale, Georgia Ponsonby and Maia Roos had all recommended it, having had stints there.

World.title: Kyrgios provisionally suspended after positive cocaine test in Spain
World.content:
Australian tennis star Nick Kyrgios has said he tested positive for cocaine on the Spanish island of Mallorca and has issued an apology.

In a statement on his Instagram, he announced he "made a huge mistake and I take full responsibility for it".

"I'm sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me," Kyrgios said.

"Above all I'm sorry to the kids who follow me.

" I know the example this sets and I'm deeply disappointed with myself. "

The International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) issued a statement revealing Kyrgios had been "provisionally suspended" since August 4.

"31-year-old Kyrgios provided a sample during an ATP 250 event in Mallorca, Spain, on 22 June 2026," it said.

"On 17 July 2026, a World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)-accredited laboratory confirmed the presence of benzoylecgonine, a metabolite of cocaine."

"Kyrgios, who reached a career-high world singles ranking of 13 in October 2016, has the right to appeal the provisional suspension, but has not done so to date," the ITIA said.

"As with all Tennis Anti-Doping Programme cases, ITIA support is available to Kyrgios.

"While suspended, Kyrgios is not allowed to play in, coach at, or attend any events organised or sanctioned by World Tennis, WTA, ATP, the Grand Slams, or any national association."

Nick Kyrgios has been open with his struggles with mental health in the past, including with depression and suicidal ideation. (Reuters: Amr Alfiky)

Kyrgios explained the incident came in the context of years "of injuries … both physically and mentally".

"My body hasn't been able to do what my mind expects it to do, and coming to terms with being near the end of my career has been harder than I ever imagined."

Kyrgios has spoken publicly about his previous struggles with mental health, telling the BBC in 2022 he struggled with alcohol and drug abuse, as well as depression and self-harm.

He has won seven ATP singles titles and the 2022 Australian Open doubles title, partnering with Thanasi Kokkinakis.

In July 2026, he lost in the first round of men's doubles at Wimbledon and later said it was probably his last appearance at the competition.

"I would probably say pretty confidently my last Wimbledon," Kyrgios said.

"It would be hard to see myself coming back here again and competing.

"That [2022] final was always going to be one of the better memories of my tennis career, but I just can't see myself getting back to anywhere near that level.

"I've always said I didn't choose tennis, tennis chose me," Kyrgios said.

"But letting go of something that has been my whole life is one of the hardest things I've ever had to face.

" At times I've felt helpless and alone. None of that excuses what I did. "

He said the "good news" was his drug test failure and suspension "has given me a wake-up call" and said he would step away from social media and the public spotlight for the next 28 days.

"I'd ask that people respect my privacy during that time, and most importantly the privacy of my family," he said.

"I'm sorry.

"I'll do the work and come back better."

World.title: 'We are deeply sorry': Swans players break silence over alleged incident
World.content:
Five Sydney Swans players who were stood down for the rest of the season over breaches of club standards have issued an apology to their club, fans and the wider community.

In a statement on behalf of Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Isaac Heeney, James Jordon and Chad Warner, the players said they were "deeply sorry to everyone involved".

The players were banned by the Swans for breaches of standards and expected behaviour after they stayed out late drinking and brought women back to the team hotel after the game against Essendon on Sunday night.

"We know that our behaviour has fallen well short of the standards expected of us and the values of our club," they said.

The five said that they accepted the club's sanction and apologised for the impact on those involved.

Earlier in the day, the Swans said their willingness to "torpedo" their AFL season by suspending the five star players proved their commitment to upholding standards at the club.

In addition to the club sanction, the five Swans players will not be considered for All Australian selection, according to the AFL.

"Following the decision and appropriate club sanction imposed by the Sydney Swans today in relation to the conduct of five of their players, the AFL has determined those players will not be considered for selection in the 2026 All Australian squad," the league said in a statement.

"This decision is independent of the ongoing Victoria Police investigation."

Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich (left) and chairman Andrew Pridham. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Victorian detectives head to NSW

Victorian sex crime detectives are expected to travel to New South Wales as they investigate the alleged incident.

The ABC understands the investigation centres on an allegation of touching without consent at the Pullman Hotel in the early hours of Monday morning.

It is understood the alleged victim has spoken to police.

Multiple law enforcement sources have told the ABC that four officers from the Victoria Police Sex Crimes Squad will land in Sydney as they expand their investigation.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges over the alleged incident.

It is not suggested that any of the players are being accused of sexual assault, and none of the banned players has been formally interviewed by police, according to the club.

Sponsors speak out

Telstra has spoken out, saying it was "deeply concerned by what's been reported" and respected that the matter was being investigated by police.

"Players assisting police with their investigation who are also Telstra ambassadors are not participating in any ambassador activity while the investigation is ongoing," a Telstra spokesperson said.

"We will review their ambassador arrangements once the investigation is complete and will provide an update at that time."

It is understood that Heeney and Warner have both been Telstra ambassadors.

Focus should not be on 'football consequences' AFLW star turned broadcaster Kate McCarthy calls out members of the media focusing on how a police investigation linked to Sydney Swans players could affect the team's finals chances.

Swans sponsors QBE came out in support of the club's actions.

"QBE acknowledges the seriousness of the allegations that have been reported," a spokesperson said today.

"We have no tolerance for conduct that compromises the safety, dignity or wellbeing of others and we support the club's position in condemning all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women.

"Given there is an active police investigation it would be inappropriate for us to comment any further."

Another club sponsor, realestate.com.au, also responded, saying they were "deeply concerned about the serious allegations involving several Sydney Swans players".

"We are aware there are investigations currently being conducted by the relevant authorities and await the findings of those investigations," a company spokesperson said.

Swans sanctions solely for breaches of club standards

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham and chief executive Matthew Pavlich have stressed the decision to ban the players is solely related to breaches of the club's standards and expected behaviour.

"Hopefully people can see how seriously we've taken this matter," Pridham said.

"We're very proud of our culture we've built over many years at the club. We get more right than we get wrong. Clearly this is a very sad day for us and for everybody involved.

"I know the five players involved, they're extremely remorseful for their actions in breaching the club's standards, and I think the sanction we've imposed and the impact that will have on our football season is clear for all to see.

"It's very important to note the football outcome was not a consideration of the board."

Loading...

Sydney's sanctions came after the club conducted interviews with the players linked to the Melbourne incident off-site with their lawyers present. Sydney's board met on Tuesday night to discuss club-imposed sanctions.

The bans handed to the players, according to the club bosses, relate to their decision to continue drinking late into the night and bring women back to the hotel.

Pavlich said it fell "a long way short of what we expect of our players", and Pridham added that their actions left the club with no choice but to impose a heavy sanction.

"They shouldn't have been in that situation," Pridham said.

"The only way we can deal with it is to put our foot down incredibly hard, which we've done. To effectively torpedo our season by making a decision such as this tells you how seriously we're taking this."

The AFL has backed the team's sanctions and the Swans say their decision is independent of an ongoing Victoria Police investigation.

The rest of the Swans will prepare for North Melbourne on Sunday and then a finals campaign. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The players' ban includes this Sunday's home-and-away finale against North Melbourne and any finals matches the Swans will play afterwards.

Pavlich said the club was "deeply embarrassed and ashamed", stressing they were "deeply concerned" about the welfare and wellbeing of the women involved.

"They're the ones who are impacted severely at the moment," he said, adding that the Swans did not want to interfere with the police investigation by reaching out to the women directly.

While the five suspended players will not be allowed to play for the rest of the year, Pavlich said "they will be allowed back at the football club" this season.

"We're not abandoning our players," he said.

"We are supporting our players through this really challenging time for them."

Pridham pointed out the sanctions should not tarnish the entire team's reputation.

"There are many players this doesn't apply to, and I believe our male team has, by and large, displayed complete respect for women, so I don't think that's something of concern," he said.

"However, clearly when situations such as this emerge, and clearly there has been a breakdown in standards, we will, in time, as a board and as an executive team, review how we deal with these things going forward and we'll look to see if changes need to be made.

"We're very, very proud of our culture. We don't get everything perfectly right over time, and things happen from time to time, and it's how we fix it going forward."

West Coast AFLW head coach Daisy Pearce has called on men to "be a good human" not just for themselves but for the effect they have on others. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Matt King)

AFLW pioneer Daisy Pearce says it is "disappointing" allegations of violence against women have arisen again in the AFL.

Speaking at a press conference, West Coast Eagles AFLW coach Pearce urged young men to consider how their behaviour impacted others.

"Be a good human. Be a good human and for those that are in high-profile positions understand that you being a good human matters but it also has a massive impact on what other people think is acceptable as well," she said.

World.title: Ikitau back in fray as Wallabies eye Argentina tour
World.content:
Les Kiss has resisted throwing any curveballs ahead of the Wallabies' tour of Argentina, with a fit Len Ikitau the only addition to the squad that produced wins in his first two Tests as coach.

Ikitau (ankle), the 2025 Wallabies player of the year, had minor surgery and missed the recent victories against Japan in Osaka and Townsville.

He has effectively replaced unlucky fullback Jock Campbell, who impressed in the number 15 jersey against Ireland before injuries elsewhere saw him employed as a play-making bench option against France.

With Tom Wright locked in at fullback, Campbell, who was named the Queensland Reds' best player at this week's end-of-season awards, was replaced by Ben Donaldson as the fullback or fly half bench cover for the next three Tests.

Les Kiss seeking pride The new Wallabies era under Les Kiss began with a win in tough conditions against an improving nation, but coach Les Kiss wants more than just wins to be the legacy of his tenure.

Centre Josh Flook has also been left out while Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii (hamstring) will also return after missing Saturday's Townsville Test, creating a log-jam of midfield options against the world number seven Pumas.

Winger Max Jorgensen has been included despite coming off with a sore chest on Saturday, while code-hopper Zac Lomax remains on the injury list and unavailable for selection.

Lock Miles Amatosero, unavailable for the first Test as part of a three-game suspension for a red card earned in Osaka, was also not considered for selection.

Kiss, who tested new combinations in the pack and centres in his first two games in charge, has otherwise played a straight bat ahead of what will be sterner tests in San Salvador de Jujuy and Mendoza on August 30 and September 6.

"As coaches, we've looked to maintain consistency in selection, with the bulk of this squad having laid a solid foundation over the past few weeks through their hard work and connection on and off the field," he said.

"Touring Argentina presents another tough challenge for us as a new group, and it's one that we know will require us to go to another level as we continue to look to build and develop our game."

Where Kiss selects Suaalii will be telling after Isaac Henry's strong running and second-phase play at outside centre caught the eye in Townsville.

Hunter Paisami has also impressed at number 12 in Ikitau's absence, leading to questions post-match about where Suaalii fits in the picture.

There is a push for former NRL star Suaalii to move to the wing to ensure more involvement and better harness his aerial ability.

Kiss, who replaced Joe Schmidt ahead of next year's home Rugby World Cup, said before his first Test in charge that he was "persisting at number 13 with him at this stage, but I know that he can go to fullback and wing, and that's important to acknowledge as well".

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

But Campbell and Flook's exclusion from this squad hints that Kiss is now considering a Suaalii switch.

Zane Nonggorr (calf) remains sidelined, with Massimo De Lutiis set for his first full Wallabies tour after arriving late into Osaka and debuting in Townsville.

Wright will notch 50 Test caps if he plays in both Tests.

The squad will assemble in Sydney on Saturday, before departing for Buenos Aires on Sunday.

WALLABIES SQUAD: Allan Alaalatoa, Angus Bell, Charlie Cale, Josh Canham, Massimo de Lutiis, Tom Hooper, Isaac Kailea, Fraser McReight, Josh Nasser, Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Billy Pollard, Aidan Ross, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Lachlan Shaw , Carlo Tizzano, Taniela Tupou, Rob Valetini, Jeremy Williams, Harry Wilson (c), Filipo Daugunu, Ben Donaldson, Carter Gordon, Isaac Henry, Len Ikitau, Max Jorgensen, Ryan Lonergan, Tate McDermott, Declan Meredith, Hunter Paisami, Dylan Pietsch, Harry Potter, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Kalani Thomas, Tom Wright.

AAP

World.title: Germany star says neurological issue behind two collapses in a week
World.content:
Bayern Munich midfielder Jamal Musiala has revealed a neurological issue but says he is doing well despite collapsing during a preseason game for the second time in a week.

The 23-year-old Germany international went down shortly after entering Wednesday's (AEST) friendly as a substitute in the second half. Players from both teams made a circle around Musiala as he received medical treatment. He was then helped as he walked off the pitch.

Musiala had collapsed Sunday (AEST) during a friendly against Leipzig. German news agency DPA reported he had left the field on his own but still appeared dazed.

After Wednesday's game, Musiala posted a message on his Instagram account, explaining that he had been diagnosed with temporary "but easily treatable absence seizures" caused by a neurological problem.

"These can lead to the moments that happened recently, such as against Leipzig or even now in Heidenheim," Musiala wrote.

Bayern, in its report on Wednesday's game, only said of the incident: "There was a setback when Jamal Musiala had to be subbed off with a knock minutes after coming on."

Jamal Musiala was held up by teammate Ismael Saibari (left) after fainting during Bayern's friendly against RB Leipzig. (Getty Images: Alex Grimm)

Musiala said he was "very optimistic" and was receiving excellent medical treatment.

"The important thing is that there is no additional health risk," he wrote.

"In close coordination and regular communication with experts, it has been my personal wish to face the challenge and, with the endorsement of the neurological specialists, to devote myself to what helps me most in recovery: to simply live my everyday life and keep up with my passion of playing football," Musiala added.

Bundesliga champion Bayern faces Borussia Dortmund on Sunday AEST in the German Supercup, the traditional curtain-raiser for the season.

AP

World.title: Irankunda says Hanson's monoculture comments upset team during World Cup
World.content:
Socceroos star winger Nestory Irankunda says One Nation leader Pauline Hanson's comments on multiculturalism upset many of the players during the recent World Cup.

The Australian team was competing at the tournament in North America in June when Ms Hanson made a speech at the National Press Club saying Australia should end its policy of multiculturalism in favour of a monoculture.

"It really did upset me and it upset a lot of the other boys to see things and hear things like that," Irankunda said.

" I felt a bit emotional but then tried to forget about it. "

Irankunda, who is one of several Socceroos players from a refugee background, told 702 ABC Sydney while he tried to stay off social media it was hard to avoid the senator's comments.

Loading...

"There can be some people who do the wrong thing but that doesn't mean that's all of us," he said.

"There's people like me, and Awer [Mabil], Mohamed Touré that go out there. There's a lot of boys like us that go out there and do the right thing.

"I don't like how they try and put us in the whole same category as the other people who do bad."

Irankunda was born in a refugee camp in Tanzania in 2006 to Burundian parents who fled the nation's civil war. He came to Australia when he was three months old.

Irankunda was speaking with presenter Hamish Macdonald on 702 ABC Sydney just days after moving from English Championship club Watford to Portuguese side Sporting CP for an undisclosed fee reported to be in the region of $26 million.

The footballer said he probably wouldn't like to speak with the One Nation senator as he was still upset by the comments and "some of the things she said in the past".

"I'm not someone that likes to jump into controversial things or this political stuff. But I mean, you know, you never know," Irankunda said.

"One day I could be on the phone with her or sitting in an office chatting to her. So I mean … we'll see what happens."

Pauline Hanson's speech at the National Press Club included a call to end Australia's decades-old policy of multiculturalism. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

After her press club speech, Hanson said the Socceroos represented her vision of a monocultural Australia.

"People from different background and cultures and nations all wearing the green and gold and representing one nation under one flag and succeeding under the same set of rules," Hanson said in the Senate in June.

Socceroo Awer Mabil addressed the monoculture debate when he returned in July from the tournament, declaring his team was not distracted and that it was "all bullshit" to suggest Australia was not a multicultural society.

Australian team destined to 'go far'

Irankunda said despite the Round of 32 loss to Egypt, the Socceroos had youth on their side and could go further into the tournament.

"You can see now with the likes of Lucas Herrington, Ali [Alessandro] Circati, Jordy Bos, you know, Mohamed Touré, all these names, all these young boys coming through, including myself," Irankunda said.

"There's still a lot of talent coming through in Australia right now.

"Only time will tell how far we can go. But I feel like in my heart that we can go pretty far."

World.title: Victorian detectives to head to NSW as Swans hotel investigation expands
World.content:
Victorian sex crime detectives are expected to travel to New South Wales as they investigate an alleged sex assault scandal engulfing the Sydney Swans.

The ABC understands the investigation centres on an allegation of touching without consent at the Pullman Hotel in the early hours of Monday morning.

It is understood the alleged victim has spoken to police.

Multiple law enforcement sources have told the ABC that four officers from the Victoria Police Sex Crimes Squad will land in Sydney as they expand their investigation.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges over the alleged incident.

Earlier today the Swans said their willingness to "torpedo" their AFL season by suspending five star players proves how committed they are to upholding standards at the club.

The Swans suspended Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Isaac Heeney, James Jordon and Chad Warner for the remainder of the 2026 AFL season over an alleged incident at a Melbourne hotel in the early hours of Monday morning.

At least five players were linked to an ongoing Victoria Police investigation into an alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel, where the Swans were staying after their win over Essendon on Sunday night.

It is not suggested that any of the players are being accused of sexual assault and none of the banned players have been formally interviewed by police, according to the club, or charged.

In addition to the club sanction, the five Swans players will not be considered for All Australian selection, according to the AFL.

"Following the decision and appropriate club sanction imposed by the Sydney Swans today in relation to the conduct of five of their players, the AFL has determined those players will not be considered for selection in the 2026 All Australian squad," the league said in a statement.

"This decision is independent of the ongoing Victoria Police investigation.

The AFL said the 2026 All Australian squad would be finalised on Monday next week, with the team announced at the AFL Awards the next day in Melbourne.

Telstra has spoken out, saying it was "deeply concerned by what's been reported" and respected that the matter was being investigated by police.

"Players assisting police with their investigation who are also Telstra ambassadors are not participating in any ambassador activity while the investigation is ongoing," a Telstra spokesperson said.

"We will review their ambassador arrangements once the investigation is complete and will provide an update at that time."

It is understood that Heeney and Warner have both been Telstra ambassadors.

Swans sponsors QBE came out in support of the club's actions.

"QBE acknowledges the seriousness of the allegations that have been reported," a spokesperson said today.

"We have no tolerance for conduct that compromises the safety, dignity or wellbeing of others and we support the club's position in condemning all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women.

"Given there is an active police investigation it would be inappropriate for us to comment any further."

Another club sponsor, realestate.com.au, also responded, saying they were "deeply concerned about the serious allegations involving several Sydney Swans players".

"We are aware there are investigations currently being conducted by the relevant authorities and await the findings of those investigations," a company spokesperson said.

Swans sanctions solely for breaches of club standards

(Clockwise from top left) James Jordon, Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner and Isaac Heeney have been stood down. (ABC News/Getty Images)

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham and chief executive Matthew Pavlich have stressed the decision to ban the players is solely related to breaches of the club's standards and expected behaviour.

"Hopefully people can see how seriously we've taken this matter," Pridham said.

"We're very proud of our culture we've built over many years at the club. We get more right than we get wrong. Clearly this is a very sad day for us and for everybody involved.

Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich (left) and chairman Andrew Pridham. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

"I know the five players involved, they're extremely remorseful for their actions in breaching the club's standards, and I think the sanction we've imposed and the impact that will have on our football season is clear for all to see.

"It's very important to note the football outcome was not a consideration of the board."

Sydney's sanctions came after the club conducted interviews with the players linked to the Melbourne incident off-site with their lawyers present. Sydney's board met on Tuesday night to discuss club-imposed sanctions.

Focus should not be on 'football consequences' AFLW star turned broadcaster Kate McCarthy calls out members of the media focusing on how a police investigation linked to Sydney Swans players could affect the team's finals chances.

The bans handed to the players, according to the club bosses, relate to their decision to continue drinking late into the night and bring women back to the hotel.

Pavlich said it fell "a long way short of what we expect of our players", and Pridham added that their actions left the club with no choice but to impose a heavy sanction.

"They shouldn't have been in that situation," Pridham said.

"The only way we can deal with it is to put our foot down incredibly hard, which we've done. To effectively torpedo our season by making a decision such as this tells you how seriously we're taking this."

The AFL has backed the team's sanctions and the Swans say their decision is independent of an ongoing Victoria Police investigation.

The rest of the Swans will prepare for North Melbourne on Sunday and then a finals campaign. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The players' ban includes this Sunday's home-and-away finale against North Melbourne and any finals matches the Swans will play afterwards.

Pavlich said the club was "deeply embarrassed and ashamed", stressing they were "deeply concerned" about the welfare and wellbeing of the women involved.

"They're the ones who are impacted severely at the moment," he said, adding that the Swans did not want to interfere with the police investigation by reaching out to the women directly.

While the five suspended players will not be allowed to play for the rest of the year, Pavlich said "they will be allowed back at the football club" this season.

"We're not abandoning our players," he said.

"We are supporting our players through this really challenging time for them."

Pridham pointed out the sanctions should not tarnish the entire team's reputation.

"There are many players this doesn't apply to, and I believe our male team has, by and large, displayed complete respect for women, so I don't think that's something of concern," he said.

"However, clearly when situations such as this emerge, and clearly there has been a breakdown in standards, we will, in time, as a board and as an executive team, review how we deal with these things going forward and we'll look to see if changes need to be made.

"We're very, very proud of our culture. We don't get everything perfectly right over time, and things happen from time to time, and it's how we fix it going forward."

West Coast AFLW head coach Daisy Pearce has called on men to "be a good human" not just for themselves but for the effect they have on others. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Matt King)

AFLW pioneer Daisy Pearce says it is "disappointing" allegations of violence against women have arisen again in the AFL.

Speaking at a press conference, West Coast Eagles AFLW coach Pearce urged young men to consider how their behaviour impacted others.

"Be a good human. Be a good human and for those that are in high-profile positions understand that you being a good human matters but it also has a massive impact on what other people think is acceptable as well," she said.
